nodes.label: Concept
nodes.text: Concept The database (SQL) is the core every data career passes through (Excel → SQL → Python → Data Analyst / Data Engineer / Data Scientist). Following Grok's principle — the black hole is never drawn, only the light around it — the database is not drawn as a shape; it is the void at the centre of a disc of light. The void is the "unknown" that data science and AI explore; the three traced layers make it read instantly as a database.

nodes.text: Construction (viewBox `0 0 100 100`) ```svg <svg viewBox="0 0 100 100" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"> <circle class="disc" cx="50" cy="50" r="46" fill="#f4f4f4"/> <path class="void" d="M29 31C29 17 71 17 71 31V69C71 83 29 83 29 69Z" fill="#000"/> <g class="bands" fill="none" stroke="#f4f4f4" stroke-width="4" stroke-linecap="round"> <path d="M29 31C29 45 71 45 71 31"/> <!-- top rim --> <path d="M29 45C29 59 71 59 71 45"/> <!-- layer 1 --> <path d="M29 59C29 73 71 73 71 59"/> <!-- layer 2 --> </g> </svg> ``` Keep the class names (`disc`, `void`, `bands`) — the animation depends on them.

nodes.label: Usage rules
nodes.text: Usage rules - Default: white logo on black. Use `logo-light-bg.svg` only on light surfaces. - The void must always be the background colour (it is a hole, not a black shape). On a non-black background, use the inline version and set `--logo-bg` to that background. - Minimum size 16 px. Clear space around it = ¼ of its width. - No outlines, glows, gradients, rotation or added elements (stars, sparkles were tried and removed on purpose). - Wordmark: datafromzero, lowercase, Geist 500, letter-spacing −0.01em, to the right of the mark; tagline *From A1 to AI* in Geist Mono when space allows. ---

Use `gsap.matchMedia()` for reduced-motion and pointer checks, and kill ScrollTriggers on page leave if client-side navigation is enabled. - Starlight config: use `logo/logo-dark-bg.svg` as the site logo (with a light-theme variant `logo-light-bg.svg` if light mode is kept) and `logo/favicon.svg` as the favicon. Two modes: - Study / lessons: open, quiet, one idea per screen, generous spacing. - Reference: book-like, indexed, searchable (Starlight's built-in search), compact. - Math: DS / Statistics pages need LaTeX — add `remark-math` + `rehype-katex` (and KaTeX CSS). - Fonts: self-host or use Google Fonts with `display=swap`; preload Geist 400 and, on the homepage, Geist 500 (the hero wordmark). - Performance budget: JS before first paint ≈ 3 KB gzipped, effects loaded on demand (SPEC D28); no images required — everything is SVG/CSS. nodes.label: 1. The project this package serves
nodes.text: 1. The project this package serves Data From Zero is a free, visual-first learning site that teaches its own original content. The path shape is already decided and is not reopened by this research: - One linear path: Excel → SQL (one complete block) → Python → advanced core → five career tracks. - The five tracks: Data Analyst, Data Engineer, Data Scientist, Analytics Engineer, ML/AI Engineer. - Free in full. No paywall, no account wall for reading and learning, no free-tier funnel. The whole path is the product. - Visual-first teaching. Each core concept gets a canonical visual or interactive demonstration, not just prose and code. - Bilingual-ready by structure: English at the root, Vietnamese under `/vi/`. The Vietnamese edition is scaffolding — terminology, examples, and format guidance built for Vietnamese learners — not a machine translation of the English pages. - Repo as source of truth. Site content lives as Markdown in the repository; a sync step mirrors it into the website. A published page's URL does not change; a rename requires a redirect. Later owner decision (2026-11-17, SPEC D32): the site has four career tracks. Analytics Engineer is no longer a track; its skills live in Data Engineer and Data Analyst. The research below predates that decision and is kept as written. Judge every recommendation in this package against four tests from the project charter: does it beat the incumbents on clarity, on visual and intuitive teaching, on time-to-skill, and on caree…

nodes.text: 2.10 Kaggle Learn and the practice layer — teach, drill, simulate The free and practice-first ecosystem splits cleanly into three jobs, and no single resource does more than one of them well: - Teach. Kaggle Learn offers 17 free micro-courses (Python, Pandas, visualization, cleaning, Intro and Advanced SQL against BigQuery datasets, an ML ladder from intro through intermediate, feature engineering, explainability, deep learning, and specialties). Each course is a handful of short tutorials paired with auto-checked exercise notebooks on real data, and Intro to ML exits directly into a competition submission. SQLBolt teaches SQL basics in 18 lessons — one concept, then in-browser queries on a single small dataset, no account, no paid tier — and stops exactly where analyst interviews start: no window functions, no CTEs. The Mode SQL Tutorial (now hosted by ThoughtSpot after acquisition; any published link must use the live destination and be re-checked) teaches analyst-style SQL anchored to business questions, up through window functions and session analysis, without auto-grading or progress tracking. W3Schools is the reference layer: short pages with a runnable example beside every explanation, free to read, with depth capped at light-intermediate. - Drill. HackerRank's SQL and Python domains run judged challenges from Easy to Hard, and its free certifications publish the clearest public ladder in this layer — Basic (simple queries, relationships, aggregators), Intermediate (c…

nodes.label: 2.11 roadmap.sh — the map that teaches nothing
nodes.text: 2.11 roadmap.sh — the map that teaches nothing Positioning. Free, community-created visual roadmaps: 62 skill roadmaps listed on the homepage, including Data Analyst, BI Analyst, Data Engineer, Machine Learning, AI and Data Scientist, SQL, Python for Data Analysis, and Power BI. Clicking a node leads out to scattered external resources. Why it spreads. The developer-roadmap repository is the distribution case study of this whole map: a single visual artifact that is screenshot-able, printable, and forwardable, with share badges shipped in the README itself. The UI audit scores its visual teaching aids 5 of 5 and its syllabus transparency 5 of 5 — for the map. The same audit states the trade-off plainly: the chart tells the learner what and in what order, but teaches nothing by itself. There are no datasets, no drills, no time estimates, no difficulty gradient, and no non-English edition of substance. The gap it defines. roadmap.sh owns "map, no teaching." DataCamp owns "teaching, paywalled, English-first." The open position is the intersection: an open map whose every node opens a real, visual, bite-size lesson in a set order. That is the position §5 builds on.

nodes.label: 2.12 WorldQuant University — the free accredited pole
nodes.text: 2.12 WorldQuant University — the free accredited pole Positioning. A not-for-profit, fully online university in Washington, D.C., founded in 2015 and funded by the WorldQuant Foundation. Accredited by the Distance Education Accrediting Commission (DEAC, a US national accreditor — a real distinction from regional accreditation for credit transfer and some employers), with initial accreditation in 2021. The model is completely free, not merely tuition-free: no tuition, no application fee, no examination fees, and no fee for the degree, certificate, or verified credential itself. The only possible learner cost is an external English-proficiency test paid to its provider. Portfolio. Two families. Graduate Programs are for-credit, cohort-based, and run on a fixed calendar: an MSc in Financial Engineering (39 credits, nine courses plus capstone, gated by a bachelor's degree, English proficiency, and a Quantitative Proficiency Test score of 75% or higher; 20–25 hours per week over about two years), a Graduate Certificate in Applied AI Fundamentals (15 credits, five courses, no coding — AI tools and dashboards for decision-makers), and an MSc in Strategic AI and Innovation (30 credits, ten courses) that stacks directly on the certificate, gated by an 80% program average. Labs are not for credit, are fully self-paced and project-based, and carry no pathway into the degrees: Data Foundations (8 projects total, 2 units of 4 — the FAQ figure governs; see `00-README.md` §4), Data Science…

nodes.label: 2.13 OSSU — the curate-a-degree pole
nodes.text: 2.13 OSSU — the curate-a-degree pole Positioning. The Open Source Society University creates no teaching material. Each GitHub repository is a curated, ordered list of free courses from universities and MOOC platforms, assembled to mirror an undergraduate degree and maintained by a named maintainer plus community pull requests. Learners fork the repo and tick off completed courses in their own copy — the fork count is simultaneously a user metric and a distribution artifact — and gather in Discord and GitHub issues. The Data Science path explicitly follows the American Statistical Association's undergraduate data-science curriculum guidelines. Scale (date-stamped, per the honesty rules). The Computer Science repository stands at about 211K stars, November 2026 (211,134 stars read directly on 2026-11-15; the live counter had already drifted by +2 within roughly a day of the Wave 4 check, which is why the package uses the approximation). The Data Science repository stands at about 22K stars on the same basis. Brand spillover matters: the flagship CS repo lends credibility to the much smaller DS repo (144 commits versus the CS repo's 1,112 — the DS path is visibly the less-maintained sibling). Shape. About 2 years at about 20 hours per week. Prerequisites are high school mathematics plus prior statistics. The Data Science path runs eleven sections: orientation, MIT's Python sequence, a four-course data-structures-and-algorithms block taught in Java, a databases section framed a…

nodes.label: 2.2 Coursera — the credential marketplace
nodes.text: 2.2 Coursera — the credential marketplace Positioning. Career credentials carrying the Google, IBM, Meta, and university brands, with shareable certificates, Credly badges, and — for several programs — ACE and FIBAA recommendations worth up to 12 US college credits and 6 ECTS, subject to each receiving institution. Google certificates plug into an employer consortium (150+ US employers named on the page); IBM certificates plug into IBM's Talent Network. Scale and the contradiction finding. Coursera's own pages disagree about its own programs, and Wave 4 re-verified that the disagreement is real and still present. It is a finding about the platform, not a research error: - Google Data Analytics: Coursera's program page states 9 courses and over 180 hours; Google's own grow.google page lists 8 courses and about 240 hours; a tally of Coursera's own course cards sums to about 152 hours. Three official-ish numbers for one program. - IBM Data Analyst: 11 courses in the current V3 version (older issued badges show 9 courses), about 151 learning hours. Use the versioned formulation; do not drop the version note. - IBM Data Engineering: the current listing enumerates 16 courses ending with generative-AI and career-guide courses, while the badge criteria text attaches about 217 learning hours to a 13-course set, and older marketing pages describe 13 courses with timelines up to 12–15 months. State the count and the hours as two separately sourced, versioned facts — never as the single…

nodes.label: 2.3 Dataquest — sequencing as the product
nodes.text: 2.3 Dataquest — sequencing as the product Positioning. No videos at all. Every lesson is a short concept followed immediately by code written and checked in the browser against real datasets. Paths are fully sequenced so the learner never decides what comes next, and path pages state courses, projects, hours, and enrolled learners up front. Scale. Eight career paths in the catalog listing: Junior Data Analyst (19 courses, 15 projects, 97 hours; Excel first, then SQL, then Python), Data Analyst in Python (27 courses, 19 projects, 144 hours), Data Analyst in R, Data Scientist in Python (38 courses, 27 projects, 171 hours), Data Engineer (30 courses, 14 projects, 81 hours), AI Engineer in Python (the most current AI curriculum among the interactive platforms: LLM APIs, prompt engineering, embeddings, vector databases, RAG, FastAPI deployment), and Business Analyst paths for Power BI and Tableau tied to vendor certifications. The homepage shows slightly different counts for two paths; the catalog figures above are the more detailed listing. Dataquest's own comparison article puts the full catalog at 109 courses across career and skill paths. Strengths. The highest practice density of the paid interactive platforms; guided projects interleaved through each path rather than saved for the end (19 in the analyst path); honest time math that converts path length into months at 5 versus 10 hours per week; the clearest beginner information architecture in the UI audit (beginner clarity…

nodes.label: 2.4 Codecademy — structure plus career tooling
nodes.text: 2.4 Codecademy — structure plus career tooling Positioning. Interactive lessons, quizzes, and projects organized into career paths, skill paths, and courses, wrapped in career services: a job-readiness checker that scores skills against a job posting, an AI interview simulator, and interview-preparation skill paths. Architecture worth noting. The three Data Scientist paths (Machine Learning, Analytics, Inference) share one foundations trunk — data literacy → SQL (at unit 3, before deep Python) → Python fundamentals → pandas → EDA → statistics → visualization → portfolio projects — and then branch into a specialty. The Inference specialty goes furthest on statistics of any platform in this trio: hypothesis testing, regression for inference, and causal inference, plus R. Path pages publish units, lessons, projects, quizzes, and total hours before signup (the Inference path: 24 units, 78 lessons, 59 projects, 53 quizzes, about 85 hours). Portfolio projects land mid-path, not only at the end. Weaknesses. Career paths run roughly 50–95 hours — breadth and speed over depth compared with Dataquest's 81–200. The entire career-relevant catalog sits behind Plus/Pro; certificates are a paid-plan feature, and a skill-path page states plainly that starting requires upgrading the plan. There is no dedicated data-engineering career path, Excel appears only as a unit inside two paths, and the headline project counts are inflated by many small exercises rather than substantial builds. The id…

nodes.label: 2.5 freeCodeCamp — free, but the data track is archived
nodes.text: 2.5 freeCodeCamp — free, but the data track is archived Positioning. A donor-funded nonprofit where everything — lessons, projects, exams, and publicly verifiable certificates — is free. Certification means completing learning blocks plus five required projects with automated tests. The structural fact. The current recommended curriculum is web-development-first. The data certifications most learners know (Data Analysis with Python, Machine Learning with Python, Scientific Computing with Python) have been moved to an archive: still available and claimable, flagged on every page as no longer updated. The maintained on-ramps are a general Python certification and a Relational Databases certification. Coverage. The archived data-analysis certification covers Jupyter, NumPy, pandas, cleaning, and reading data, ending in five projects; visualization is Matplotlib and Seaborn. SQL lives only inside the developer-flavored Relational Database line (Bash and terminal first, then PostgreSQL and Git, in a real dev environment) — not taught as an analyst skill in sequence with Python. ML is a single TensorFlow-centric video course with no scikit-learn-first progression and no LLM content. There is no Excel, no BI tooling, no dedicated statistics, and no data-engineering path. The legacy data certifications also lean on long passive video, unlike the interactive-challenge model of the web-dev side. Why it still matters. It is the trust benchmark for any free competitor: zero price includ…

nodes.label: 2.6 Udemy — the marketplace long tail
nodes.text: 2.6 Udemy — the marketplace long tail Positioning. Anyone can publish; the market sorts by ratings and reviews. Learners either buy a course once with lifetime access (list prices roughly $20–$200, with near-constant sales bringing most courses to about $10–$20) or subscribe to a curated Personal Plan (26,000+ courses, advertised from about $13 per month). Certificates of completion are not accredited. Depth pockets no structured platform matches. Spreadsheet craft as a profession: the flagship Excel course (about 23 hours) runs through Microsoft 365 dynamic-array functions, Power Query, PowerPivot and the data model, and macros/VBA with project work. Database design taught as its own subject, side by side across SQL Server and PostgreSQL. A flagship ML course that implements every topic three ways (Python, R, and a cloud track) and includes reinforcement learning and association rules that structured curricula omit or thin out. All-in-one analyst bootcamps (one opened example: about 89 hours) that bolt Python, statistics, SQL, Power BI, and a capstone into a single product — and keep bolting on new tool modules, including generative AI, as the market moves. Weakness. The marketplace structurally cannot answer the beginner's first question — what order? Thousands of near-duplicate courses with instructor-varying quality is the opposite of a committed sequence. Data engineering has no dominant flagship at all, only tool-specific and exam-prep courses with no sequencing guidan…

nodes.label: 2.7 edX — the university model
nodes.text: 2.7 edX — the university model Positioning. Universities and companies supply stacked credentials: single courses → Professional Certificates → MicroMasters → online master's degrees. Most courses audit free; payment buys graded work and the verified certificate. MicroMasters sequences can convert into credit toward a partner university's master's. Depth pockets. The deepest standalone statistics and math bench in this map: MIT's Statistics and Data Science MicroMasters runs semester-length probability (15–17-week courses) with a proctored capstone exam; Stanford's Statistical Learning sits alongside it. UC San Diego's Data Science MicroMasters ($1,260 for the program in the pages opened) and Georgia Tech's Analytics MicroMasters ($2,475; the same foundational courses as its online MS in Analytics) show the graduate end of the market. HarvardX's Data Science certificate teaches the whole discipline in R — a deliberate differentiator — and uniquely treats productivity tooling (Unix, Git and GitHub, reproducible documents) as first-class curriculum. Adelaide's Big Data MicroMasters ($985.50) leads with computational thinking and algorithm design rather than tools. Weakness. Excel is thin and SQL is rarely a standalone headline; both live embedded inside broader programs. This is not where the market learns analyst-grade spreadsheet or querying depth, and semester pacing with instructor-paced cohorts is the opposite of self-serve reference content. Note also that MIT's MicroMas…

nodes.label: 2.8 Pluralsight — diagnostics and certification depth
nodes.text: 2.8 Pluralsight — diagnostics and certification depth Positioning. A curated, subscription-only tech library of vetted expert authors, organized into sequenced paths wrapped with Skill IQ adaptive assessments, hands-on labs and sandboxes on higher tiers, and certification practice exams. There is no per-course purchase; canceling ends access. The 2026 plan structure is modular (a core library plus stackable deep libraries, with a Complete plan); exact price points are region- and promotion-sensitive and the tier system was replaced in 2026, so this map records the structure rather than a single price. Depth pockets. Certification-aligned engineering content written to vendor exam blueprints (Azure data engineering sequences, Microsoft Fabric, Snowflake operations taught as scaling, monitoring, and governance rather than just queries). An enterprise BI long tail — Qlik Sense, MicroStrategy, Alteryx — alongside Tableau and Power BI. Its own career guidance sequences analyst → data science → data engineering → MLOps as one lattice with SQL named as the baseline skill for every role. The idea worth stealing. Assessment-first routing: a diagnostic score places the learner at the right level of a path instead of forcing a fixed lesson 1. No fixed-track rival in this map does this. Data From Zero's checkpoint-gated linear path is a different answer to the same problem — one committed order, with gates — but the underlying insight (placement beats assumption) is shared.

nodes.label: 2.9 LinkedIn Learning — the workplace library
nodes.text: 2.9 LinkedIn Learning — the workplace library Positioning. In-house-produced, practitioner-taught video courses organized into career learning paths, with certificates that attach directly to the learner's LinkedIn profile — the profile hook is the real product. Individuals reach it through LinkedIn Premium (US pricing shown at $39.99 per month or $239.88 per year in the pages opened); employers buy per-seat licenses, and many public libraries provide it free. Distinctive coverage. It productized analytics engineering as a named job title early: a dedicated course built around the data lifecycle, SQL for analytics engineering, Python and pandas for the role, and dbt as the centerpiece transformation tool. Its analyst path opens with non-technical skills — soft skills sequenced inside a technical path, not offered as blog advice — and covers Copilot-assisted Excel analysis. Its ML paths include explainable AI, causal inference, and no-code ML in KNIME and SPSS Modeler: the enterprise GUI toolchain that code-first platforms exclude entirely. Weakness. Path assembly seams show: the analyst path ends with a Python data-cleaning course that assumes Python the path itself never teaches. Depth is workplace-upskilling grade — aimed at professionals improving in place — rather than career-switcher mastery, and there is no single flagship Python-for-data sequence comparable to the marketplace bestsellers.

nodes.label: 3. Paywall and free models compared
nodes.text: 3. Paywall and free models compared Five distinct models appear in this map, and the differences matter more than the prices: 1. Sampling funnel (DataCamp, Coursera, Codecademy). A deliberately incomplete free experience — first chapter, first module, or selected courses — designed to convert. The free tier is a demo, not a plan. Codecademy's version is the least candid: a course can be free to start while its projects, assessments, and certificate are revealed as paid in a block at the bottom of the course page. 2. Intro-free, core-paid (Dataquest). Introductory content of every path free with no credit card, stated plainly, with honest completion math — the most candid paid model in the map — but full paths, projects, and certificates still behind a subscription whose price the public pages do not show. 3. Marketplace and library pricing (Udemy, edX, Pluralsight, LinkedIn Learning). Per-course purchase with perpetual discounting; free audit with a paid verified track; modular subscription libraries with no single-course purchase; and bundling into a broader professional subscription, respectively. In all four, the beginner's problem is not only price but legibility: what to buy, in what order, and what it adds up to is genuinely hard to determine from public pages. 4. Fully free with a credential (freeCodeCamp, Kaggle Learn, WQU). The credential itself costs nothing. The three differ in everything else: freeCodeCamp's data track is archived, Kaggle's courses are deliberate…

nodes.label: 4. Cross-cutting structural findings
nodes.text: 4. Cross-cutting structural findings These findings recur across platforms and are stated once here rather than repeated per profile. 1. Recycling creates repetition. DataCamp reuses the same SQL, Python, and statistics courses across its analyst, data-science, and ML tracks; Coursera reuses the same IBM courses across four certificates, and its FAQ confirms a course completed once counts everywhere. Breadth on the shelf is partly the same content re-sequenced. A single canonical lesson graph — learn once, credit everywhere across the path and tracks — is a genuine design advantage, not a slogan. 2. One course template, reused at scale, is the incumbents' unit economics. DataCamp's roughly 4-hour course (four chapters, video alternating with in-browser exercise) is reused across 810+ courses; tracks are pure sequencing plus projects and assessments. Beating the incumbents does not require out-producing the catalog. It requires beating the template and the sequencing in the domains learners start with: Excel, SQL, and Python. 3. Projects are the differentiator incumbents lean on — and the consensus finish line. Flagship career tracks carry 2–9 projects on realistic datasets; freeCodeCamp requires five per certification; Dataquest interleaves up to 27 guided projects per path; WQU Labs are nothing but projects. Independently, hiring-side research in this package converges on the same standard: a portfolio of 3–5 finished projects beats a stack of certificates (with Data Engine…

nodes.label: 5. Gaps Data From Zero exploits
nodes.text: 5. Gaps Data From Zero exploits In priority order. Each gap names the structural reason incumbents cannot close it quickly.

nodes.label: Gap 1 — The free + deep quadrant is empty
nodes.text: Gap 1 — The free + deep quadrant is empty freeCodeCamp is free but its data track is archived and missing Excel, BI, statistics depth, and data engineering. Kaggle Learn is free but deliberately shallow. WQU is free and deep but selective, finance-tilted, and slow. roadmap.sh and OSSU are free maps to other people's paywalls. Dataquest is deep and well sequenced but paywalled; Codecademy is well structured but paid and light. A free roadmap with Dataquest-grade sequencing, Codecademy-grade structure, and full depth in Excel, SQL, Python, and statistics occupies a quadrant no incumbent currently holds. Incumbents cannot follow without cannibalizing the subscription the funnel exists to sell; the one nonprofit that could (freeCodeCamp) would have to un-archive and rebuild a data track it has deprioritized in favor of web development.

nodes.label: Gap 2 — Visual teaching is the unclaimed differentiator
nodes.text: Gap 2 — Visual teaching is the unclaimed differentiator The UI audit's visual-teaching scores: roadmap.sh 5 of 5 for its map only (a navigation chart that teaches nothing); DataCamp, Dataquest, Codecademy, and Kaggle Learn at 4; freeCodeCamp at 3; Coursera at 2. No platform leads with concept-level visuals — a canonical diagram or interactive for joins, window functions, distributions, regression, or ML intuition — inside the lesson itself. Data From Zero's premise is exactly that: the map from roadmap.sh, the openness from freeCodeCamp, the card metadata from Dataquest, and a real visual lesson behind every node. The build catalog, costs, and priority order for those visuals are in the teaching playbook and UI lessons files.

nodes.label: Gap 3 — Vietnamese scaffolding is a moat, not a translation feature
nodes.text: Gap 3 — Vietnamese scaffolding is a moat, not a translation feature Wave 4 verified the incumbents' current position against their own official pages. DataCamp now offers Vietnamese through AI-plus-human-review translation, explicitly in beta, covering courses, assessments, practices, projects, and interface — with partner courses English-only and a lower AI-tutor-only tier whose wider platform stays in English. Coursera's auto-translation covers 4,000+ courses in 40 additional languages including Vietnamese, but its own support page lists what is not translated: downloadable files, externally hosted assignments, peer-graded submissions and feedback, hands-on labs and guided projects, and other learners' discussion posts. Dataquest and Codecademy are English-only. In other words, the translated layer stops exactly where the assessed, hands-on learning happens. The moat is therefore not translation — the incumbents are closing that gap mechanically — but scaffolding built for Vietnamese learners from the start: a terminology rule and glossary that keep job vocabulary in English while explaining in Vietnamese; localized Vietnam-context examples, datasets, and salary framing (entry-level analyst pay in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi listed at 10–16 million VND per month in the Vietnamese career guide opened in this research, against US-dollar subscriptions priced for US and EU professionals); and format guidance for the traps that actually bite — Excel function names are not locali…

nodes.label: Gap 4 — One committed order, with gates, against the catalog
nodes.text: Gap 4 — One committed order, with gates, against the catalog The most repeated beginner question in the community evidence is not "what is SQL" but "what do I learn first, and in what order?" — and the most named drop-off pattern is tutorial hell: weeks jumping between courses with no order and no checkpoints. A marketplace structurally cannot answer the order question, because its business is the catalog; a track-selling platform cannot tell learners to ignore 99% of its catalog. Data From Zero's answer is one line — Excel → SQL (one complete block) → Python → advanced core → one of five tracks — with week-sized stages and a "you may proceed when you can do X" gate at each stage. The demand evidence (§4.7) validates the specific order; the learning-sequence argument (build on the spreadsheet fluency business-background switchers already have, instead of restarting them at HTML or generic code) validates it independently.

nodes.label: Gap 5 — Job tasks and a portfolio as the finish line, localized
nodes.text: Gap 5 — Job tasks and a portfolio as the finish line, localized Incumbents sell certificates, so they cannot demote certificates below portfolios without devaluing their own product — yet the hiring-side evidence says portfolios are what employers screen for, and their examples, datasets, and salary data are US-market. Data From Zero ends every stage in workplace artifacts (a monthly sales report, a churn query, a dashboard a manager could read) and ends the path in 3–5 portfolio projects, with the Data Engineering exception of 2–3 deep projects, framed against the Vietnamese job market. External proof points are named and linked (free HackerRank certificates, LeetCode's SQL 50 and pandas plans, Kaggle competitions) rather than imitated.

nodes.label: Gap 6 — An open, forkable roadmap the community can improve
nodes.text: Gap 6 — An open, forkable roadmap the community can improve The two open artifacts in this map — roadmap.sh's map and OSSU's fork-and-tick-off curriculum — are also its two proven distribution engines: a free, ordered, GitHub-native artifact is content other creators make videos about, and every learner's fork is a public progress tracker and an advertisement at once. Incumbent content lives inside closed platforms optimized for enrollment, not remixing; opening it would break their licensing and funnel metrics. Data From Zero publishes under CC BY 4.0, so teachers and creators may legally re-share and re-teach the material, and layers a named public challenge pattern (daily public progress, in the #100DaysOfCode mold) on top so learners distribute the path themselves. The full positioning moves and shareability mechanics are in `05-career-and-viral.md`. ---

nodes.text: 6. Confidence and sourcing note Platform structure, path sequences, and catalog counts in this file rest on primary pages opened on 2026-11-15 and, for the 30 highest-risk claims, re-verified in Wave 4 (19 confirmed, 7 partially confirmed, 2 unverified, 2 contradicted — both contradicted items being inconsistencies inside the sources themselves; see `00-README.md` §4). Pricing is the least stable layer: every vendor in this map discounts aggressively and rotates promotions, so every price here carries its checked date and should be re-checked before any public republication. nodes.label: 1. Stage 1 — Spreadsheets and the BI Layer
nodes.text: 1. Stage 1 — Spreadsheets and the BI Layer Source: `syllabus-excel-bi.md` — Microsoft Excel (Part A), Google Sheets (Part B), BI concepts (Part C), Tableau (Part D), Power BI (Part E). Three tiers run through the stage in dependency order: Beginner (first job tasks), Working (independent analyst), Advanced (power user / BI developer).

nodes.label: 1.1 Excel — interface, hygiene, and formula foundations
nodes.text: 1.1 Excel — interface, hygiene, and formula foundations - Workbook navigation and editing: ribbon, name box, formula bar, copy/paste and Paste Special, Fill Series and Flash Fill, multiple sheets and workbooks, number formats, freeze panes and print setup. - Data-hygiene rules that every later stage assumes: one header row, one fact per cell, no merged cells in data, no blank rows or columns inside a dataset, raw data kept separate from calculations and outputs. - Sheet and workbook protection and workbook properties. - Formula writing: operators and order of operations; relative, absolute, and mixed references and what happens when a formula is copied; named ranges and the Name Manager; structured references inside Excel Tables. - Error literacy and auditing: the common error values, tracing precedents and dependents, Evaluate Formula, Watch Window, Show Formulas.

nodes.label: 1.2 Excel — function families
nodes.text: 1.2 Excel — function families - Math and statistics: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, and the COUNT family; conditional aggregation with SUMIF(S), COUNTIF(S), AVERAGEIF(S); ROUND family, INT, MOD; SUBTOTAL and AGGREGATE on filtered data; SUMPRODUCT; MEDIAN, MODE, standard deviation and variance (sample vs. population), PERCENTILE, QUARTILE, RANK; LARGE, SMALL, MAXIFS, MINIFS; CORREL and first-pass regression functions (SLOPE, INTERCEPT, RSQ; LINEST at awareness level); database functions and RAND/RANDBETWEEN at awareness level. - Logic: IF, nested IF and IFS, AND/OR/NOT, IFERROR and IFNA, SWITCH and CHOOSE; the flag-then-aggregate pattern (build a label column, then count or sum by it). - Lookup and reference: XLOOKUP as the current default; VLOOKUP and HLOOKUP for reading legacy workbooks; INDEX + MATCH including two-way lookups; MATCH match types and approximate-match behavior; CHOOSE, OFFSET, INDIRECT at awareness level with caution; ROW/COLUMN family; joining datasets on a unique key as the spreadsheet rehearsal for SQL joins. - Text: LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LEN; TEXTBEFORE, TEXTAFTER, TEXTSPLIT; CONCAT and TEXTJOIN; TRIM, CLEAN, UPPER, LOWER, PROPER; FIND, SEARCH, SUBSTITUTE, REPLACE; TEXT for formatting and VALUE/DATEVALUE/TIMEVALUE for conversion back; regular-expression functions at awareness level; EXACT at awareness level. - Date and time: dates as serial numbers; TODAY, NOW, DATE and date-part functions including WEEKDAY and week numbers; EDATE and EOMONTH; DATEDIF and subtracti…

nodes.label: 1.3 Excel — working with data
nodes.text: 1.3 Excel — working with data - Tables, sorting, and filtering: converting a range to an Excel Table; single- and multi-level sorting and custom sort lists; AutoFilter; Advanced Filter at awareness level; Remove Duplicates and Consolidate at awareness level; Text to Columns. - Conditional formatting: highlight-cell rules, top/bottom and above/below-average rules, data bars, color scales and icon sets, formula-based rules that format a whole row, and rule management. - Data validation: whole-number, decimal, date, and text-length validation with messages and alerts; dropdown lists; dependent dropdowns; formula-based custom validation; circling invalid data in an inherited sheet. - PivotTables and PivotCharts: building from a clean Table; changing aggregation and number format; grouping dates, numbers, and text; sorting, filtering, top-10 and value filters; Show Values As (share, difference, running total, rank); slicers and timelines; calculated fields and items at working level; refresh discipline and GETPIVOTDATA at awareness level; linked PivotCharts; drill-down to detail. - Charts and presentation: column/bar, line, and pie/doughnut charts and when each is honest; combo charts with a secondary axis; scatter and bubble charts at working level; titles that state the takeaway, axis formatting, legends and gridline restraint; sparklines; dynamic chart ranges from Tables and named ranges; in-cell alternatives at awareness level.

nodes.label: 1.4 Excel — cleaning, modern functions, and automation-adjacent tools
nodes.text: 1.4 Excel — cleaning, modern functions, and automation-adjacent tools - End-to-end cleaning workflow: profile before cleaning (blanks, duplicates, distinct values, type mismatches); standardize keys; handle missing values deliberately and document the choice; split and merge columns; convert types safely and check after conversion; resolve duplicates by full row and by key; replace inconsistent labels via a mapping table; keep raw data, cleaned data, and a change log. - Dynamic arrays (Microsoft 365): spill ranges and the #SPILL! error; FILTER; SORT, SORTBY, UNIQUE; SEQUENCE and RANDARRAY at working level; TAKE, DROP, CHOOSECOLS, CHOOSEROWS, HSTACK, VSTACK, TOCOL/TOROW; LET for readable long formulas; LAMBDA with BYROW/BYCLO/MAP/SCAN/REDUCE at advanced awareness level; combined XLOOKUP + FILTER + UNIQUE reporting patterns. - Power Query in Excel: Get Data from files, folders, the web, and other sheets; core editor transformations (remove/rename/reorder, types, filter, sort); split/merge columns, replace values, fill down, trim/clean; unpivot and pivot; merge queries with explicit join types; append queries; Group By; parameters and folder refresh at advanced level; reading and lightly editing M code at advanced awareness level; loading to a Table or the Data Model and refreshing on open. - What-if, Solver, and forecasting: Goal Seek; one- and two-variable Data Tables; Scenario Manager; Solver at working level; Forecast Sheet and FORECAST.ETS / FORECAST.LINEAR at working leve…

nodes.label: 1.5 Google Sheets — what transfers, what is Sheets-only
nodes.text: 1.5 Google Sheets — what transfers, what is Sheets-only - Direct transfer: core formula families, PivotTables, charts, conditional formatting, data validation, named ranges, and protected ranges work in Sheets with different menus; Explore, filter views, and slicers. - Sheets-only power features: QUERY (SQL-like selection over a range, and a gentle on-ramp to Stage 2); ARRAYFORMULA with MAP/LAMBDA; IMPORTRANGE; IMPORTDATA, IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML; GOOGLEFINANCE; SPARKLINE; REGEXMATCH, REGEXEXTRACT, REGEXREPLACE; UNIQUE, FILTER, SORT, SORTN, FLATTEN, TRANSPOSE; DETECTLANGUAGE and GOOGLETRANSLATE at awareness level; sharing, comments, version history and restore; Connected Sheets and BigQuery-linked tables at awareness level; the in-cell AI function at awareness level, with its output verified like any unverified draft (see Section 7).

nodes.label: 1.6 BI concepts that precede any tool
nodes.text: 1.6 BI concepts that precede any tool - Operational reports vs. dashboards vs. self-service BI; the pipeline connect → clean/transform → model → calculate → visualize → publish/refresh. - Facts vs. dimensions and the star schema; grain stated for every table before joining; keys and relationships, one-to-many and many-to-many hazards, cross-filter direction; measures (aggregated on the fly) vs. stored columns; refresh, scheduling, and visible data-freshness labels.

nodes.label: 1.7 Tableau
nodes.text: 1.7 Tableau - Foundations: dimensions vs. measures, discrete vs. continuous; connecting to files, databases, and cloud sources; live connection vs. extract; the Data pane (rename, alias, default formats, geographic roles, hierarchies, folders); first views for comparison, trend, composition, and correlation; sorting, grouping, sets, and bins; filter types and the order of operations. - Calculations and analysis: row-level and aggregate calculated fields; quick table calculations (running total, percent of total, difference, percent difference, rank, moving average); addressing and partitioning; LOD expressions (FIXED, INCLUDE, EXCLUDE); parameters and parameter actions; reference lines, bands, distributions, trend lines, and simple forecasting; blending, relationships, joins, and unions; Tableau Prep Builder flows at working level. - Dashboards, stories, and publishing: layout containers and device layouts; dashboard actions (filter, highlight, URL, parameter); stories as sequenced arguments; publishing to Tableau Server / Cloud with permissions and extract refresh schedules; Tableau Public as portfolio proof; performance hygiene at advanced level; Tableau Certified Data Analyst blueprint at awareness level.

nodes.label: 1.8 Power BI
nodes.text: 1.8 Power BI - Get and prepare: connecting Power BI Desktop to files, folders, databases, and web sources; Power Query transformations (the same engine and M language as Section 1.4); Import vs. DirectQuery vs. composite models at working level. - Modeling: star schema design; relationships, cardinality, and cross-filter direction; active vs. inactive relationships; hiding keys and technical columns, display folders, formats and types; hierarchies and drill-down paths. - DAX: measures vs. calculated columns vs. calculated tables; core aggregation and iterator functions including DISTINCTCOUNT; filter context and row context; CALCULATE with ALL / ALLEXCEPT / REMOVEFILTERS; time intelligence (TOTALYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, DATEADD, DATESINPERIOD) with a marked date table; variables (VAR … RETURN); visual calculations at awareness level; USERELATIONSHIP and role-playing dimensions at advanced level; row-level security roles at advanced level. - Visuals, reports, and publishing: core visuals and formatting discipline; cross-highlighting, drill-through, tooltips, bookmarks, and buttons; conditional formatting in tables and matrices; publishing to the Power BI service (workspaces, apps, sharing, permissions); scheduled refresh and gateways; the PL-300 domain list at awareness level (cross-reference in Section 9). ---

nodes.label: 2. Stage 2 — SQL, One Complete Block
nodes.text: 2. Stage 2 — SQL, One Complete Block Source: `syllabus-sql.md`, sections 0–17 plus its completion standard (260+ items). Teach in the order shown; a later block assumes the earlier blocks. Three depth labels run through the block in the source: Core (analysts and data scientists), Working (data/analytics engineers and advanced analysts), Awareness (recognize and know when to look it up).

nodes.label: 2.1 Foundations and retrieval (source sections 0–3)
nodes.text: 2.1 Foundations and retrieval (source sections 0–3) - Relational model: database, schema, table, row, column, value; primary keys and foreign keys; one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many relationships; result grain stated before writing a metric. - Query anatomy and logical order of execution (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT); schema discovery through catalogs and information_schema; safe previewing with a row limit; readable formatting, comments, and statement boundaries. - Retrieval: named columns vs. SELECT * and its risks; column and table aliases; qualified names; literals; arithmetic expressions and operator precedence; DISTINCT on one and on multiple columns; stable output column order. - Filtering: equality and inequality, range comparisons, AND/OR/NOT with parentheses, BETWEEN and half-open date ranges, IN and NOT IN lists, LIKE with % and _, IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, case sensitivity and collation, filtering on calculated conditions, sargable filter shapes, WHERE vs. HAVING. - Sorting and limiting: ORDER BY on one column, several columns, and expressions; ASC/DESC; NULLS FIRST/LAST where supported; LIMIT and OFFSET; deterministic tie-breakers; FETCH FIRST; dialect sampling syntax; pagination cost awareness.

nodes.label: 2.2 Aggregation and joining (source sections 4–5)
nodes.text: 2.2 Aggregation and joining (source sections 4–5) - Aggregates: COUNT(*) vs. COUNT(column) vs. COUNT(DISTINCT …); SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX; GROUP BY on one key, several keys, and expressions; HAVING; aggregate behavior with NULL; conditional aggregation and FILTER (WHERE …) where supported; percentages and ratios with the correct denominator; percent of total; median and percentile functions per dialect; string, array, and boolean aggregation; ROLLUP, CUBE, and GROUPING SETS; grouping-key validation. - Joins: join keys and cardinality prediction; INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, and CROSS joins; multiple joins in one query; composite keys; non-equi (band) joins; temporal and as-of joins; self-joins; anti-joins (LEFT JOIN … IS NULL and NOT EXISTS); semi-joins (EXISTS and IN); join fanout and pre-aggregating the many side before joining; USING shorthand; why NATURAL JOIN is risky; join-condition placement in ON vs. WHERE.

nodes.label: 2.3 Composition (source sections 6–8)
nodes.text: 2.3 Composition (source sections 6–8) - Subqueries and CTEs: scalar subqueries; subqueries in WHERE with IN, ANY/SOME, and ALL; EXISTS; derived tables; subqueries in SELECT; correlated and nested subqueries; single and multiple dependent CTEs; CTE reuse; recursive CTEs (hierarchies, category trees, date spines); CTE vs. subquery choice; CTE materialization awareness; LATERAL joins where supported; debugging a CTE pipeline stage by stage. - Set operations: UNION vs. UNION ALL; column count, order, and type compatibility; INTERSECT; EXCEPT (MINUS in Oracle-oriented material); precedence and parentheses; sorting a combined result; set operations vs. joins and vs. OR. - Conditional logic: searched and simple CASE; ordered and nested branches; CASE inside aggregation, for numeric bucketing, for standardization, in ORDER BY, and for pivot-style columns; ELSE defaults; unmatched branches returning NULL; CASE with aggregate conditions; short-circuit caveats.

nodes.label: 2.4 Functions, windows, and missing data (source sections 9–11)
nodes.text: 2.4 Functions, windows, and missing data (source sections 9–11) - String functions: length, case conversion, trimming, concatenation, substring and left/right extraction, position-finding, REPLACE, SPLIT_PART, splitting and unnesting, pattern matching and regular expressions, padding, and parsing emails, URLs, and UTM parameters. - Date and time functions: current date/time anchors; EXTRACT / DATE_PART; DATE_TRUNC; interval addition and subtraction; date differences and age; date construction; parsing text to dates with an explicit format; formatting for export; time-zone conversion; month-boundary logic; incomplete-period awareness. - Math and general scalar functions: arithmetic and modulo; ABS; CEIL and FLOOR; ROUND and truncation; POWER, SQRT, EXP, LOG; GREATEST and LEAST; safe division with NULLIF; COALESCE for display defaults and for sentinel cleanup; random functions; JSON extraction; array membership and unnesting where supported. - Window functions: OVER, PARTITION BY, and window ORDER BY; ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE, PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST; LAG and LEAD with offsets and defaults; FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE (including its default-frame trap), NTH_VALUE; running totals, counts, averages, minima, and maxima; moving averages with ROWS BETWEEN; RANGE and GROUPS frames; default frame semantics; named WINDOW definitions; filtering on a window result through an outer query or CTE; share of partition total; window functions after grouping; cumulative distinct-count l…

nodes.label: 2.5 Types, writing data, and performance (source sections 12–14)
nodes.text: 2.5 Types, writing data, and performance (source sections 12–14) - Data types and casting: integer, DECIMAL/NUMERIC for money, floating point and approximation, text types, booleans and engine substitutes, DATE, TIME, timestamp with and without time zone, INTERVAL; UUID, binary, JSON, array, and spatial types at awareness level; CAST and the PostgreSQL :: shorthand; implicit-conversion risks; integer-division differences; date-parsing ambiguity; collation; SQLite type affinity and strict-typing differences; read-time generated values vs. stored generated columns. - Defining and changing data: CREATE SCHEMA and CREATE TABLE; single and composite primary keys; foreign keys and referential actions (RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL); NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and DEFAULT constraints; identity/serial/autoincrement keys; generated columns; ALTER TABLE; DROP TABLE; TRUNCATE vs. DELETE; INSERT (one row, many rows, INSERT INTO … SELECT); UPDATE with a restrictive WHERE and UPDATE from another table; DELETE with a restrictive WHERE; upserts (ON CONFLICT, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, MERGE); RETURNING where supported; views and materialized views; temporary tables; CREATE TABLE AS SELECT; transactions (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK) and savepoints; ACID at awareness level; normalization to 1NF–3NF and deliberate denormalization into star schemas. - Indexes and performance: what an index does and the B-tree mental model; single-column, composite (with column order), unique, partial, expression, and cov…

nodes.label: 2.6 Dialects, analytic patterns, and production checks (source sections 15–17)
nodes.text: 2.6 Dialects, analytic patterns, and production checks (source sections 15–17) - Dialect differences that change real work: identifier quoting and case folding; fully qualified warehouse names; row limiting; string concatenation; case-insensitive matching; boolean representation; date/time, string, division, cast, upsert, changed-row output, recursive CTE spelling, window-function availability by version, FULL OUTER JOIN and set-operation availability, identity generation, JSON and nested data, native pivot support, QUALIFY, temporary and materialized objects, regular-expression syntax, date-spine generation, and error/warning behavior — across PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and BigQuery, with SQL Server forms recognized in inherited code. - Analytic patterns: a metric contract before SQL (numerator, denominator, grain, date field, time zone, inclusion rules); source profiling; reconciliation totals; complete time series on a date spine; period-over-period, year-over-year, and rolling metrics; funnel definition, ordered funnels, conversion and drop-off, session-constrained funnels; cohort assignment by first event, retention matrices, and retention denominator control; churn, reactivation, and resurrection flags; exact-duplicate and key-based deduplication with stated survivorship rules; latest record per entity; top-N per group with an explicit tie policy; pivoting and unpivoting; Pareto and cumulative-share analysis; RFM segmentation; basket and attach-rate analysis; distribut…

nodes.label: 3. Stage 3 — Python for Data Work
nodes.text: 3. Stage 3 — Python for Data Work Source: `syllabus-python.md`, sections 0–15 plus its cut list. Learners arrive able to think in tables, filters, joins, and aggregations; this stage re-teaches those instincts in code. The source flags explicit bridges from Excel and SQL, and a cut list of widely taught beginner material demoted because working data roles rarely use it at this level.

nodes.label: 3.1 Foundations (source sections 0–9)
nodes.text: 3.1 Foundations (source sections 0–9) - Setup and notebooks: running Python in the browser with zero install; notebook anatomy (code vs. Markdown cells, top-to-bottom execution, kernel restart); cell state and execution order; saving, sharing, and exporting notebooks; print and last-expression display; local setup (Python, VS Code, Jupyter) as a later optional step. - Core syntax: variables and assignment; int, float, str, bool, and None; dynamic typing and type(); arithmetic, comparison, and boolean operators; input() and conversion with int(), float(), str(); comments. - Strings: literals, quotes, and escapes; indexing and slicing; the working method set (strip, lower/upper, replace, split, join, startswith, find, membership); f-strings for formatted reporting; string immutability. - Conditionals: if/elif/else; nested conditions and when to flatten them; truthiness; ternary expressions. - Loops and comprehensions: for loops, range(), while loops with an infinite-loop warning, break and continue, enumerate() and zip(), list comprehensions as the stage's central idiom, and dict/set comprehensions in one line each. - Data structures: lists (indexing, slicing, append, sort, membership); tuples and immutability; dictionaries (get with a default, keys/values/items, building from data) as the structure of JSON and of DataFrame construction; sets (uniqueness, intersection/union/difference); choosing list vs. dict vs. set; sorting with key= and lambda. - Functions, modules, and pac…

nodes.label: 3.2 NumPy and pandas (source sections 10–11)
nodes.text: 3.2 NumPy and pandas (source sections 10–11) - NumPy: why arrays exist under pandas; creating arrays (array, arange, linspace, zeros/ones, reshape); shape, dtype, ndim; indexing, slicing, and boolean masking; vectorized arithmetic and universal functions including np.where; broadcasting; aggregation axes; random numbers with a seed for reproducible sampling, shuffling, and simulation. - pandas structures and first contact: Series and DataFrame; building a DataFrame from a dict and from a list of dicts; reading CSV, Excel, JSON, and SQL; the first-look toolkit (head, tail, info, describe, shape, columns, dtypes); writing CSV and Excel. - Selection and filtering: column selection; loc (labels) vs. iloc (positions); boolean filtering with &, |, ~ and parentheses; isin, between, and query; sort_values; adding, renaming, and dropping columns. - Grouping and aggregation: groupby as split-apply-combine; agg with several statistics and named aggregations; multiple grouping columns; pivot_table as the reproducible form of the Stage 1 pivot; value_counts; cumulative, rolling, and shifted calculations. - Combining tables: merge with how= inner/left/right/outer, validate= for relationship checks, and indicator= for diagnosing row changes; concat for stacking files; index join at recognition level. - Reshaping and tidiness: melt (wide to long) and pivot/pivot_table (long to wide); stack/unstack at recognition level; explode; get_dummies for one-hot encoding; MultiIndex at recognize-and-f…

nodes.label: 3.3 Visualization, workflow, APIs, and automation (source sections 12–15)
nodes.text: 3.3 Visualization, workflow, APIs, and automation (source sections 12–15) - Visualization: figure vs. axes as the one mental model; pandas plotting for a first chart; matplotlib essentials (line/bar/scatter, titles, labels, saving a figure); chart choice by question; seaborn one-liners on tidy data with hue= for grouped comparison; reading a chart critically (truncated axes, chartjunk, misleading bins). - Workflow skills: virtual environments and pip (taught after the browser phase); requirements.txt; Git and GitHub basics (clone, add, commit, push, pull, reading a diff); reading documentation and help; asking AI tools well and verifying the answer by running it; project organization (data / notebooks / outputs, dated file names); notebook fluency including restart-and-run-all before sharing. - APIs and web data: what an API is; HTTP request/response and status codes at concept level; requests.get and reading JSON into dicts/lists; query parameters and API keys kept out of shared notebooks; pagination at concept level; json_normalize from response to DataFrame; scraping awareness through read_html for public tables, with terms and ethics, in one lesson. - Automation and reporting: turning a notebook into a runnable .py script; parameterizing a script at the top; the batch pattern (loop over a folder, clean each file, concat, write one output); scheduled refresh at concept level; automated reporting (Excel/CSV output, a chart image, and a short Markdown/HTML summary in one ru…

nodes.label: 3.4 Python cut list (from the source, kept as scope decisions)
nodes.text: 3.4 Python cut list (from the source, kept as scope decisions) The source demotes the following from Stage 3 core to a later stage, a sidebar, or recognition level only: hand-implemented data structures and sorting algorithms (linked lists, trees, merge sort by hand); OOP depth (inheritance design, dunder methods, properties); decorators, generators, and advanced *args/kwargs; full regular-expression theory; match statements; pytest and unit testing as a module (one awareness lesson on assertions and spot checks instead); NumPy linear-algebra implementation depth; MultiIndex mastery; deep web-scraping frameworks; matplotlib styling internals. The algorithmic consequences of this list are stated explicitly in Section 8. ---

nodes.label: 4. Advanced Core, Part 1 — Statistics, Analytics, and Data-Science Foundations
nodes.text: 4. Advanced Core, Part 1 — Statistics, Analytics, and Data-Science Foundations Source: `syllabus-stats-analytics-ds.md`, sections 1–14 (about 120 items). This inventory is the advanced core for every track and the foundation of the Data Scientist track. Items are in dependency order. The source marks with an opening flag the topics where competitors are weakest — typically formula-first, intuition-light, or skipped — including observational-vs-experimental design, base-rate reasoning, correct confidence-interval interpretation, p-value misreadings, survivorship and missing-not-at-random traps, and Simpson's paradox. Those flags are preserved in substance below because they set teaching priority, not extra topics.

nodes.label: 4.1 Design, description, and visualization judgment (source sections 1–3)
nodes.text: 4.1 Design, description, and visualization judgment (source sections 1–3) - Data types and study design: categorical vs. numerical, discrete vs. continuous; levels of measurement; observational study vs. experiment; confounders and lurking variables; random assignment vs. random sampling as two different jobs; association is not causation at the design stage; units, rows, and grain; data provenance. - Descriptive statistics and distributions: frequency and relative-frequency tables; mean vs. median vs. mode and when each misleads; range, IQR, variance, standard deviation; percentiles, quartiles, and box plots; shape (skewness, modality, symmetry); outlier detection plus the keep/remove judgment; z-scores and standardization; the normal distribution and the empirical rule; binomial, Poisson, uniform, and exponential distributions at recognition level; comparing distributions across groups on center, spread, and shape together. - Visualization judgment: chart choice by question type; what bar, line, scatter, histogram, and box plots are each for; truncated axes, dual axes, and cherry-picked windows; aggregation hiding the story; displaying uncertainty (error bars, bands, sample-size annotation); sorting, labeling, and direct annotation; color discipline including colorblind safety; dashboard vs. exploratory plot.

nodes.label: 4.2 Probability, sampling, and inference (source sections 4–7)
nodes.text: 4.2 Probability, sampling, and inference (source sections 4–7) - Probability foundations: sample spaces, events, addition and complement rules; independent vs. dependent events and the multiplication rule; conditional probability read in both directions; Bayes' theorem as belief updating with base rates first; discrete vs. continuous random variables; expected value; variance of a random variable; law of large numbers at intuition level; permutations and combinations at recognition level. - Sampling and bias: population vs. sample, parameter vs. statistic; simple random, stratified, cluster, and systematic sampling; convenience and voluntary-response samples; the bias taxonomy (selection, nonresponse, survivorship, measurement); sampling variability and sampling distributions; the Central Limit Theorem, intuition first; standard error vs. standard deviation; sample size and margin-of-error trade-offs. - Confidence intervals: point vs. interval estimates; correct interpretation of a 95% interval as long-run coverage; intervals for a proportion and for a mean (t-interval); margin of error and what shrinks it; bootstrap intervals for statistics with no neat formula; confidence interval vs. prediction interval. - Hypothesis testing, taught honestly: null and alternative as competing claims; what a p-value is and the three things it is not; significance level and the Type I / Type II trade-off; power and what raises it; one- and two-sample t-tests, paired vs. independent; proport…

nodes.label: 4.3 Experimentation, causation, and regression (source sections 8–10)
nodes.text: 4.3 Experimentation, causation, and regression (source sections 8–10) - A/B testing end to end: from business question to one primary metric; primary, guardrail, and vanity metrics; randomization unit and assignment; sample-size and power analysis before launch; minimum detectable effect as a business choice; running discipline (fixed horizon, no peeking, no mid-test changes); sanity checks (sample-ratio mismatch, instrumentation, seasonality, weekday effects); analyzing means and proportions; ratio metrics and the delta method at recognition level; novelty and primacy effects and long-term holdouts; the ship / no-ship decision memo; Bayesian A/B testing at recognition level. - Correlation vs. causation: the correlation coefficient and its limits; the three rival explanations (reverse causation, confounder, coincidence) as a checklist; spurious correlation and data dredging; Simpson's paradox; the ecological fallacy; regression to the mean; what earns causal language (randomization, natural experiments, difference-in-differences at recognition level, mechanism and dose-response). - Regression as a thinking tool: slope and intercept as a story; least squares and residuals; R² and its limits; reading coefficients with units and baselines; multiple regression as controlling for other variables; categorical predictors and dummy variables; logistic regression (log-odds, odds ratios, predicted probabilities); assumptions and diagnostics; multicollinearity at recognition level; ext…

nodes.label: 4.4 Analytics craft and communication (source sections 11–14)
nodes.text: 4.4 Analytics craft and communication (source sections 11–14) - Metrics, funnels, cohorts, and retention: metric design and gaming resistance; north-star vs. input vs. health metrics; rates vs. counts vs. ratios and denominator choice; funnel analysis (step conversion, drop-off, time between steps); cohort analysis separating age effects from calendar effects; retention curves and churn definitions (logo vs. revenue, voluntary vs. involuntary); segmentation including RFM; customer lifetime value, CAC, and the LTV:CAC ratio; seasonality and year-over-year comparison; anomaly triage (data, real, or us — in that order); instrumentation and event taxonomy basics; data-quality checks inside analysis. - Storytelling and stakeholder communication: starting from the decision, not the dataset; one headline takeaway per chart; narrative structure (context, tension, evidence, recommendation); translating statistical output into business language without losing uncertainty; anticipating hostile questions; documenting method and caveats without burying the answer; agreeing the question and success criteria before analyzing. - Spreadsheet-to-code workflow: the spreadsheet mental model as the bridge to SQL and pandas; cleaning as a first-class step; reproducibility through scripts and notebooks over manual edits; the analyst's loop (question → extract → wrangle → summarize → visualize → communicate); versioning and documenting an analysis; when to stay in a spreadsheet vs. move to code. -…

nodes.label: 4.5 Visualization as a learner skill — extraction note
nodes.text: 4.5 Visualization as a learner skill — extraction note No single source file owns visualization as one inventory; the topic lines are dispersed across Section 1 of this file (Excel charts, Tableau, Power BI), Section 4.1 above (visualization judgment), and the Python visualization topics in Section 3.3. [Recommendation, following the Wave 4 dedupe note] The build should present those lines as one visible visualization strand — chart choice, honest axes and aggregation, uncertainty display, dashboard composition, and tool execution in Excel, Python, Tableau, and Power BI — extracted from the sections above, not researched or listed separately a second time. ---

nodes.label: 5. Advanced Core, Part 2 — How the Core Assembles Before the Track Split
nodes.text: 5. Advanced Core, Part 2 — How the Core Assembles Before the Track Split The advanced core is not a sixth topic list. It is the point in the path where the earlier stages are combined and completed before learners split into the five tracks: - The BI layer of Stage 1 completed at working level: BI concepts (Section 1.6), one BI tool in depth (Tableau in Section 1.7 or Power BI in Section 1.8), and the modeling ideas both tools reward — star schema, grain, relationships, measures vs. columns. - The full statistics and analytics inventory in Section 4, including experimentation, causation, regression, product-analytics craft, and stakeholder communication. - The AI-era concepts module in Section 7 (retrieval-augmented generation and agents as literacy, evaluation basics, and evaluating "chat with your data" products), placed here because it assumes SQL, Python, and a formed verification habit. - A cross-tool end-to-end case in the analyst's loop from Section 4.4: one question carried through extraction, wrangling, summarization, visualization, and a written recommendation. Project and portfolio design for that case, and for each track's capstone, is owned by the projects research (Wave 2B) and is not listed here. Track entry expectations follow directly: the Data Analyst track deepens Sections 1, 4.4, and the BI layer; the Data Scientist track deepens Section 4 and Part B of Section 6; the Data Engineer and Analytics Engineer tracks deepen Part A of Section 6; the ML/AI Engine…

nodes.label: 6. Specialized Tracks — Data Engineering, Machine Learning / Deep Learning, Applied AI
nodes.text: 6. Specialized Tracks — Data Engineering, Machine Learning / Deep Learning, Applied AI Source: `syllabus-de-ml-ai.md` — Part A (Data Engineering, A0–A12, serving the Data Engineer and Analytics Engineer tracks) and Part B (Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Applied AI, B0–B12, serving the Data Scientist and ML/AI Engineer tracks), plus the source's capstone shapes and its hype-vs-fundamentals flags, preserved in substance at the end of this section.

nodes.label: 6.1 Data Engineering (source Part A)
nodes.text: 6.1 Data Engineering (source Part A) - A0 Ground rules: what a data engineer owns vs. analysts and data scientists; the data lifecycle (generate → ingest → store → transform → serve); batch vs. streaming as a business decision with a price attached. - A1 Ingestion: extracting from REST APIs (auth, pagination, rate limits); reading CSV, JSON, Parquet, and Excel defensively; incremental extraction (updated_at watermarks, change data capture at concept level); failure modes (retries, idempotent loads, dead-letter handling). - A2 Data modeling: entities, keys, and relationships in plain language; normalization (1NF–3NF) and when to break it; dimensional modeling (fact vs. dimension); star and snowflake schemas; slowly changing dimensions (Type 1 vs. Type 2); naming and grain discipline. - A3 Storage: OLTP vs. OLAP and row vs. columnar stores; data warehouse concepts; data lake concepts (object storage, schema-on-read); lakehouse and open table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg; ACID, time travel, schema enforcement); file-format trade-offs (CSV vs. Parquet vs. JSON); partitioning and clustering basics. - A4 ETL/ELT and pipeline design: ETL vs. ELT and why ELT won in cloud warehouses; pipeline anatomy (extract → stage → transform → load → serve); staging layers and the medallion pattern (bronze/silver/gold); full vs. incremental loads, upserts, and merges; backfills and safe reprocessing; idempotency as a design rule. - A5 Batch pipelines in Python: pandas for pipeline work; co…

nodes.label: 6.2 Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Applied AI (source Part B)
nodes.text: 6.2 Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Applied AI (source Part B) - B0 Framing: what ML is for (prediction under uncertainty) and what it is not; problem framing (target, unit of analysis, the decision the model feeds); classification vs. regression vs. ranking vs. forecasting; the baseline-first rule; data availability and label-quality audit. - B1 Workflow and honest evaluation: train/validation/test splits; data leakage (target leakage and train/test contamination), promoted ahead of algorithms in the source; cross-validation (k-fold, stratified, time-based); bias–variance and over/underfitting diagnosis; error analysis before model shopping. nodes.label: 6.3 Hype vs. fundamentals flags (preserved from the source)
nodes.text: 6.3 Hype vs. fundamentals flags (preserved from the source) The source flags the following as oversold in competitor syllabi, and this inventory follows its placement decisions: agents as a starting topic (here they sit after APIs, evaluation, and data plumbing); fine-tuning LLMs early (here a decision inside B10, not a default skill); prompt engineering as a standalone career skill (here one layer of B10, whose durable core is evaluation and structured output); real-time-everything streaming (here one awareness section, A10, with an explicit when-not-to item); deep learning before classical ML (here B3 precedes B8); and certificate-shaped breadth, one course per cloud service (here A11 teaches the transferable pattern — storage, orchestration, cost — on one cloud). nodes.label: 8.2 Scope decision for Data From Zero
nodes.text: 8.2 Scope decision for Data From Zero [Recommendation — explicit scope decision, stated here because the sources leave the gap open] 1. The core path (Stages 1–3, advanced core) teaches algorithmic thinking in context only: choosing a data structure, stating grain before computing, preferring vectorized and set-based operations over row loops, reading a join or sort cost at awareness level, and recognizing when a problem's size changes the right tool (spreadsheet → SQL → pandas → Spark, in the order the path itself teaches them). No Big-O formalism beyond that size intuition, and no from-scratch implementation of sorting, searching, or classic data structures, is required in the core path. 2. nodes.label: 1. The method in one page
nodes.text: 1. The method in one page Data From Zero is built against four documented failure modes in incumbent data courses: 1. Tutorial hell / the illusion of competence. [Sourced — pedagogy research] Learners finish course after course, follow every tutorial successfully, then freeze at a blank file — because the instructor made every decision (structure, names, order, debugging) and the learner practiced executing, not deciding. 2. The transfer gap. [Sourced — pedagogy research] Learners complete SQL, Python, or analytics courses, then cannot clean a messy real export, join tables that do not match a tutorial's clean schema, or answer an open-ended business question. 3. Drop-off from being stuck and from life, not from difficulty. [Sourced — pedagogy research] Completion research summarized in the research record finds non-completers cite lack of time far ahead of lost motivation or difficulty, and that dropout concentrates in the first two weeks, with speed of early completion predicting finishing better than demographics. 4. Math anxiety as an avoidance barrier. [Sourced — pedagogy research] Anxiety about mathematics drives avoidance rather than reflecting inability; platforms that front-load formulas lose learners before the applied version appears. Ten method stances answer those failures. They are stated here once, as policy; the rest of this file operationalizes them: 1. Production over recognition. No fill-in-the-blank exercise is ever a lesson's terminal exercise. Every les…

nodes.text: 2. The canonical lesson template — seven sections Total target length: 15–20 minutes for a standard lesson. [Recommendation] Lessons introducing a genuinely new mental model (first join, first groupby, first hypothesis test) may run to 25 minutes [Recommendation]; lessons extending a known pattern should run shorter, not longer. For calibration only: the research record describes incumbent lesson lengths of roughly 10–15 minutes for one video-plus-exercise platform and typically 5–10 minutes for one text-plus-code platform [Sourced].
