nodes.label: 2.1 Rules that apply to every lesson, in every domain
nodes.text: 2.1 Rules that apply to every lesson, in every domain - One new idea per lesson. [Recommendation, grounded in Sourced cognitive-load material] If a lesson needs two new ideas, it is two lessons. Combining a new concept with a new tool feature doubles intrinsic load at exactly the moment the learner has no schema for either. - Name the pattern, not just the syntax. [Recommendation] After the blank-start task, the lesson names the reusable pattern in plain language ("filter, then aggregate, then rank inside each group"), so the learner files the lesson under a *move*, not under a keyword. Interview-prep sources in the research record give the same advice: name the pattern after solving, then re-solve after the data is mutated. - Every exercise states its grain, denominator, or expected output shape before the learner starts. [Recommendation] Silent ambiguity about output shape is the most common cause of "correct work, wrong answer" in the hiring-task research. - Worked examples come in pairs for any pattern that must transfer. [Recommendation — see the mixed-evidence note in Section 1] Section 4 is the first example; Section 5, before fading bites, functions as the second. A lesson whose pattern is known to be confused with a neighboring pattern must instead use Section 4 for a side-by-side contrast pair (see the Statistics and SQL notes in Section 3). - The solution is never the first thing on the page. [Recommendation] Solutions, half-solutions, and reveal answers sit behin…

nodes.label: 3. Per-domain anatomy
nodes.text: 3. Per-domain anatomy Each domain keeps the Section 2 template and changes four things: the canonical visual, the worked-example progression across a topic, the exercise ladder, and the framing ritual the blank-start task requires. Ladders have five rungs; all rung designs, progressions, and rituals in this section are [Recommendation] unless marked [Sourced]. Topic coverage itself lives in 02-syllabus-inventory and is not reprinted here.

nodes.label: 3.1 Excel — spreadsheets first, BI concepts introduced through the sheet
nodes.text: 3.1 Excel — spreadsheets first, BI concepts introduced through the sheet Canonical visual: The sheet itself, annotated in place. For formulas: a small grid showing the formula in one cell and the values it becomes when copied down and across, with locked and moving parts in two colors. For PivotTables: the source range on the left and the pivoted result on the right, with arrows from field to area (rows / columns / values / filters). Never a screenshot of a ribbon menu as the "explanation" — menus change between versions; grid behavior does not. Worked-example progression — topic: lookups (the highest-tested Excel skill in the hiring-task research [Sourced]): 1. *Fully worked:* Bring a unit price from a reference sheet into an orders sheet by product code, where every code matches. Narration covers: why exact match is chosen deliberately, which range must stay fixed when the formula is copied, and how the result is verified (spot-check two codes by eye; total the extended amounts and reconcile). 2. *Faded:* Same task on a new file where the setup and first rows are done; the learner writes the lookup for the remaining segment and copies it correctly. One code has no match; the half-solution hint asks what the output *should* show for that row before offering any formula help. 3. *Contrast pair:* Two completed lookups side by side — one that handles the missing code deliberately (a readable "not found" result) and one that leaves a raw error value in the output column — with…

nodes.label: 3.2 SQL — one complete block, organized by pattern in its second half
nodes.text: 3.2 SQL — one complete block, organized by pattern in its second half Canonical visual: A row-flow diagram. Source tables are drawn as row stacks; each clause of the query is a gate the rows pass through — rows drop out at the filter gate, rows merge into group buckets at the aggregation gate, buckets are labeled with their computed values, then sorted. The lesson on query execution order uses this same diagram, so the visual and the execution model are one object, not two. Worked-example progression — topic: top-N per group: 1. *Fully worked:* "Top product by revenue in each category." Narration in fixed order: state the grain first (one row per category), aggregate to one row per product, rank products inside each category, keep the top rank, and state the tie policy out loud (what happens if two products tie — and which ranking function that choice implies). Verification: count the output rows and confirm it equals the number of categories. 2. *Faded:* "Second order for each customer." Aggregation and ranking steps are given; the learner writes the final selection step and the tie handling. The dataset contains a customer with only one order — the hint asks what that customer should contribute to the output before any syntax help is offered. 3. *Messy re-solve:* The step-1 problem again, but the orders table now contains duplicate rows and a missing category value. The naive query returns an inflated revenue figure. The task is to find why, repair it, and write two plain…

nodes.label: 3.3 Python — core language, then pandas as the center of gravity
nodes.text: 3.3 Python — core language, then pandas as the center of gravity Canonical visual: For core Python, a state trace: a small table showing each variable's value after each line runs, so a loop or function call is a visible change of state rather than a paragraph of prose. For pandas, the table transformation itself: the input frame drawn beside the output frame, with the rows or columns kept, dropped, grouped, or created highlighted — the same row-flow idea as SQL, drawn on dataframes. Worked-example progression — topic: grouping and aggregation in pandas: 1. *Fully worked:* Total revenue by category from a small sales frame. Narration covers: inspect the frame first (shape, types, missing values) before any computation; group, then aggregate with several named metrics in one pass; verify by reconciling the grouped total against the ungrouped total. 2. *Faded:* Share of orders by channel. Grouping is given; the learner writes the normalization step and must state whether missing channel values are inside or outside the denominator — and why. Denominator treatment in share-of-total is an explicit interview attention point [Sourced — hiring-task research]. 3. *Trap example:* Fill missing values using each row's *own group* average, shown next to the incorrect version that uses the single overall average. The two results differ visibly on the worked data; the narration explains that broadcasting a group-level value back onto rows is a distinct move from aggregating, with its own…

nodes.label: 3.4 Statistics / Analytics — the advanced core's first half
nodes.text: 3.4 Statistics / Analytics — the advanced core's first half Canonical visual: A picture of data, always before any formula. A distribution drawn as dots or bars that visibly splits when a filter is applied; a confidence interval drawn as a range over repeated samples; an A/B result drawn as two distributions with their overlap shaded. Formulas, where they appear at all, appear *after* the picture, labeled as the shorthand for what the picture shows, with an optional depth layer for learners who want the derivation. Worked-example progression — topic: "is this difference real?" (the A/B / two-group comparison): 1. *Fully worked, picture only:* Two groups' results plotted; the narration walks through a fixed diagnostic order — is the signal real (any tracking change, outage, holiday, or definition change?), then segment (platform, region, new vs. returning), then locate the driver, then state a hypothesis. No test statistic is computed in this first pass. [Order of operations Sourced — hiring-task research] 2. *Worked with numbers:* The same structure on new data, now adding the interval and the plain-language reading of it: what the interval says, and — explicitly — what a p-value is *not*. The deliverable includes the three-sentence spoken explanation the learner would give a non-technical stakeholder. 3. *Contrast pair:* Two analyses of the same experiment side by side: one that stopped early on the first encouraging result, and one that ran a full weekly cycle with primary…

nodes.label: 3.5 Data Engineering / Machine Learning / AI — the track layer
nodes.text: 3.5 Data Engineering / Machine Learning / AI — the track layer What changes at track level: The unit of a lesson is no longer a single operation; it is a *stage of a system* — one ingestion step, one transformation with tests, one stage of a modeling workflow. The worked example therefore shows a whole small system first (a handful of boxes or steps, end to end, on toy-scale data) and then zooms into one stage per lesson. A learner who has only ever seen stages in isolation cannot answer track-level interview questions, which are about how stages interact: leakage between stages, what breaks when a rerun happens, what happens when the source changes shape [Sourced — hiring-task research]. Canonical visual: For DE: a pipeline diagram with data volumes and failure points marked on the arrows, not just boxes — the arrow where duplicates enter, the arrow where a schema change lands. For ML: the workflow drawn as a one-way street with a wall between the data used to fit and the data used to judge, so leakage is a visible crossing of the wall rather than an abstract warning. For applied AI lessons: the same discipline — input, retrieval or tool step, model step, verification step — drawn as stages with the checkable artifact each stage produces. Worked-example progression — topic: DE, ingest and clean a messy file into a trustworthy table: 1. *Fully worked:* Ingest a small file with a nested field, inconsistent keys, and duplicate records. Narration covers: profile before transfor…

nodes.text: 4. Illustrative end-to-end topic: SQL joins [Recommendation — a worked illustration of the system above, not a sourced claim.] Topic: SQL joins, lessons 1–4 of the topic, topic checkpoint in lesson 5's slot. - Lesson 1 (inner joins): Recall opener reaches back to filtering and aggregation. nodes.label: 5.2 Pass rules
nodes.text: 5.2 Pass rules - Pass = production, unaided, on unseen data. [Recommendation] A checkpoint item counts as passed only if the learner produced the answer from a blank start, on data they have not seen in a worked example, without opening the full-solution layer of the help stack. Using a concept hint is permitted and noted; using the half-solution caps the item at "passed with support," which does not satisfy a gate. - Threshold: all critical items, most items overall. [Recommendation] Designate, per checkpoint, the small set of *critical* items — the ones whose failure invalidates downstream work (grain errors in SQL, reference errors in Excel, group-scope errors in pandas, definition errors in Statistics, leakage in ML). Rule: 100% of critical items and at least 4 of 5 items overall to pass a topic checkpoint; 100% of critical items at a block exit, with no compensation from other sections. Rationale: an average-based threshold lets a learner pass while carrying exactly the one misconception the next block assumes away. These numbers are design choices for Data From Zero, stated so they can be debated and changed in one place; they are not research findings. - Two attempts before intervention, then a changed strategy — not a third identical attempt. [Recommendation] Attempt 1: full checkpoint. Attempt 2: only the failed items, after completing the repair loop in Section 6. If attempt 2 fails on the same item type, the learner is routed to a *different representation* of the…

nodes.label: 5.3 What checkpoints must never do
nodes.text: 5.3 What checkpoints must never do - Never gate progress on a recognition item (multiple choice, fill-in-the-blank) alone. [Recommendation] - Never report a single percentage as the learner's state. Report the ability list: which verifiable abilities are confirmed, which are passed-with-support, which are in repair. [Recommendation] - Never let a streak, point total, or completion count substitute for a passed blank-start task. Completion-contingent rewards optimize for lesson completion, and platforms then serve easier content to protect the metric [Sourced risk — pedagogy research].

nodes.label: 5.4 Note: checkpoint resistance to AI-generated answers
nodes.text: 5.4 Note: checkpoint resistance to AI-generated answers [Recommendation — design note closing a gap flagged in the verification wave; no new research is claimed here.] Data From Zero is a free static site with no accounts and no server-side grading, so its checkpoints are self-checked by design — a learner who wants to deceive the site is only deceiving their own ability list. The design should still make honest production the path of least resistance, and make pasted answers visibly insufficient: 1. Unseen, mutated data. Checkpoint tasks use data the learner has not seen in a worked example, with surface features changed. A generated answer to the *named* pattern still has to be adapted to *this* data — and the adaptation is the skill. 2. Framing before output. Every checkpoint task requires the framing line first (grain, definition, contract, expected shape). A pasted solution without a correct framing line fails on the Framing bucket (Section 6), in the learner's own self-check. 3. Verification as a scored step. The learner must show the check — the reconciled total, the row count against the grain statement, the baseline comparison — not only the answer. Generated output rarely ships with a check that matches this dataset. 4. Narration at block exits. The written narration (assumptions, pattern chosen, validation performed) is personal to the attempt. It is also the exact artifact hiring's live rounds will demand unaided, which is the honest argument to put on the page:…

nodes.label: 6. Failure diagnosis and spaced review
nodes.text: 6. Failure diagnosis and spaced review

nodes.label: 6.1 Four failure buckets, four different repairs
nodes.text: 6.1 Four failure buckets, four different repairs Every failed checkpoint item returns a *diagnosis*, not just a mark. [Recommendation] Feedback classifies the failure into exactly one of four buckets, because each bucket has a different repair: 1. Concept — the wrong move was chosen (wrong join type, wrong denominator, wrong metric). *Repair:* re-study the canonical visual and the contrast pair for the confused patterns, then a faded example. 2. Execution — the right move, wrongly carried out (a syntax slip, a copied formula that drifted, a misordered clause). *Repair:* two rung-2 (Complete) exercises on the same pattern, then retry. 3. Framing — the work is internally correct but answers a different question (wrong grain, unstated tie policy, undefined metric, output in the wrong shape). *Repair:* rewrite only the framing line and the verification step for the failed task, explain in one sentence what the original framing got wrong, then retry the full task. This bucket exists because the hiring-task research found framing failures to be the most common *silent* failure mode — the work runs, and is wrong. 4. Verification — the answer is wrong and the learner's own check should have caught it (totals do not reconcile, row count contradicts the grain statement). *Repair:* a dedicated verification drill — three short tasks whose only job is to find the planted discrepancy — before any retry. A learner who cannot check work cannot safely work unsupervised, in any domain. Retry…

nodes.label: 6.2 Spaced review, attached to checkpoints
nodes.text: 6.2 Spaced review, attached to checkpoints - Each lesson's material re-enters the recall openers and mixed review sets on a fixed schedule. The intervals are [Recommendation]; the principle is [Sourced — pedagogy research: the spacing effect is among the most replicated findings in experimental psychology, and a simple fixed schedule captures most of the benefit of algorithmic scheduling]. Data From Zero's fixed schedule: 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 21 days after the lesson is passed. [Recommendation — these exact intervals are a design choice.] - A review item failed twice returns its lesson to "needs repair" status and inserts the Section 6.1 loop for that item's failure bucket. [Recommendation] Review is therefore not a separate game layered over the curriculum; it is the mechanism that can reopen a closed lesson. - Block exit checkpoints sample earlier blocks, not only their own: the Python exit includes SQL-pattern translations; the advanced-core exit includes one Excel- or SQL-shaped task. [Recommendation] Hiring demands the same pattern across tools, so the checkpoints must too. - Implementation on a static site: [Recommendation] the schedule renders as a "review today" page generated from the roadmap structure, plus a printable/downloadable review checklist; progress is stored in the browser only. No accounts, no server scheduler. ---

nodes.label: 7.2 House rules for every visual
nodes.text: 7.2 House rules for every visual [Recommendation throughout, synthesized from the visual-teaching research; the underlying dual-channel and split-attention principles are Sourced.] 1. Sequence: show the data moving first, name the mechanism while it is visible, show syntax or formula last, then let the learner change one thing and predict first. No hard concept is introduced by syntax or formula alone. 2. Predict-before-reveal. Before any animation or stepper advances, ask what will happen. Reveal on click. Watching becomes retrieval practice. 3. One shared visual grammar. Tables always look like tables, partitions always use the same wall style, groups always use the same buckets, a filter always uses the same chip style — across Excel, SQL, Python, and statistics. The bucket diagram for grouping is deliberately the *same artwork* in Excel pivots, SQL GROUP BY, and pandas groupby, with different syntax captions: one operation, three syntaxes. 4. Color with a job, never decoration. One color per table, per class, per partition, held constant through a whole lesson and stated in a legend. Never encode meaning in color alone — pair it with labels or patterns. 5. Small, rigged data. Every teaching dataset is tiny and deliberately loaded: a NULL key, a tie, an outlier, a duplicate — each odd row exists to make exactly one distinction visible. Realistic messy data belongs in projects; canonical visuals need data designed like a demonstration. 6. Step controls over autoplay. Play,…

nodes.label: 8.2 Terminology: the three-bucket rule and the glossary
nodes.text: 8.2 Terminology: the three-bucket rule and the glossary Bucket A — Always retain in English, never translate in running text. SQL keywords (`SELECT`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `JOIN`), Excel function names (`SUM`, `VLOOKUP`, `XLOOKUP`, `COUNTIF`), Python keywords and library names (`pandas`, `DataFrame`, `groupby`, `merge`), file formats (CSV, JSON), and error names (`#N/A`, `KeyError`, `NULL`). These are typed, searched, and read verbatim at work. Translating them in prose teaches a word the learner will never see on screen. Bucket B — Retain in English, gloss in Vietnamese on first use per lesson. Concept nouns that are also job-market keywords: *dataset, dashboard, insight, stakeholder, churn, conversion rate, outlier, median, distribution, hypothesis*. Format on /vi/ pages: English term in bold, Vietnamese gloss in parentheses on first use, English term alone after that. On EN pages: a one-line plain-English definition instead. Bucket C — Translate freely into Vietnamese. Instructional and connective language: verbs of action in exercises (calculate, compare, check, explain), business-context nouns that are not technical terms (customer, order, delivery, branch, month-end close), and all analogy / storytelling text. This is where Vietnamese does its real work — carrying reasoning, not labels. What not to do: - Do not translate a Bucket A term in a heading, button, or checkpoint answer. A checkpoint that accepts a translated keyword trains the wrong reflex. - Do not gloss the…

nodes.label: 8.3 How /vi/ pages differ beyond translation — seven ways, and only these
nodes.text: 8.3 How /vi/ pages differ beyond translation — seven ways, and only these So the two paths stay the same path, a /vi/ lesson differs from its EN counterpart in exactly these seven ways: [Recommendation] 1. An English-terms preview box at the top. The 3–6 Bucket A/B terms the lesson will use, each with its gloss, before the lesson body — so working memory at the moment the new *concept* arrives is spent on the concept, not the vocabulary. EN pages get a plainer "key terms" box with definitions — same slot, different job. 2. Worked examples narrated one step slower, with the "why" in Vietnamese. Fuller narration between steps, the mistake a beginner is about to make named *before* the step that triggers it, and a "check yourself" pause after each worked example. Local providers compete on exactly this human accompaniment; a free self-paced site bakes the accompaniment into the page. 3. Code-switching taught as a skill, not treated as a failure. Worked examples follow the daily job loop: a request in Vietnamese (a manager-style ask) → the solution in English-named tools → a Vietnamese summary sentence the learner could actually send. Each lesson ends with a "say it at work" line — Vietnamese with embedded English terms — rehearsing the reporting register, not only the tool register. A recurring /vi/-only exercise type drills reading real-shaped English error messages and documentation paragraphs: what it means, and what to do. 4. Localized examples replace, not decorate. nodes.label: 8.4 Format traps — including the Excel correction
nodes.text: 8.4 Format traps — including the Excel correction Excel function names are NOT localized for Vietnamese. [Sourced, confirmed in the verification wave] A detailed explainer on Excel across languages, opened during the research, lists the languages for which Microsoft translated function names (French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Polish, Russian, and others) and explicitly lists Vietnamese among the languages not translated. Workbook files store formulas internally in English; in Vietnamese Excel the menus and help may be Vietnamese, but the learner still types `=SUM(...)` and `=VLOOKUP(...)`. Any course material that invents Vietnamese function names is teaching fiction. All Data From Zero formulas are therefore published in English names, with no translated formula variants anywhere. [Recommendation] The real trap is the list separator and the CSV locale. [Sourced mechanism; Vietnam-specific manifestations are curriculum judgment] The same explainer confirms the mechanism: where the comma is the decimal mark, Excel uses the semicolon as the argument separator (its worked examples are European); and CSV field and decimal separators depend on the *creator's* regional settings, not on the file, so cross-locale CSVs mangle on open — the sourced guidance is to import via Power Query / From Text-CSV with explicit separator and decimal settings. Whether a given Vietnamese learner's machine expects commas or semicolons depends on their own regional settings — which…

nodes.label: 8.5 Localized example bank (summary)
nodes.text: 8.5 Localized example bank (summary) All examples are original designs — invented businesses, invented data, real Vietnam structures. Never a real company's data, a copied tutorial dataset, or a classic toy dataset. Design rules for every localized example: [Recommendation] - Money in VND, written the Vietnamese way in raw data and formatted cleanly in outputs, at realistic Vietnam scale (a single e-commerce order in the hundreds of thousands of VND; monthly store revenue in the hundreds of millions), so learners build magnitude intuition in VND rather than converting from dollars. - Names, addresses, and administrative units are Vietnamese: provinces / cities, districts, wards; phone numbers in local format as *text* (leading zero preserved — a data-type lesson in itself). - Calendars include Tet spikes, the local holidays, and the major platform sale days that dominate e-commerce data. nodes.label: 9. Anti-patterns to avoid
nodes.text: 9. Anti-patterns to avoid Each anti-pattern names the failure, its basis in the research record, and the template rule that prevents it. 1. Tutorial hell / the illusion of competence. The learner finishes course after course and freezes at a blank file, because the instructor made every decision. [Sourced — pedagogy research: the most consistently described failure pattern across learner discussions] *Prevention:* template Sections 5–6 (fading, then a blank-start task as the lesson's real test) and the Section 5.2 rule that passing requires unaided production on unseen data. 2. Fill-in-the-blank as the terminal exercise. Supplying most of the solution and asking for the last fragment produces fast, pleasant progress and learners who cannot start from nothing. [Sourced — pedagogy research] *Prevention:* fill-in formats are permitted only inside the faded example (template Section 5), never as Section 6 or as a checkpoint item. 3. Clean-data-only teaching. Every exercise on tidy, correctly typed data, so the first messy file the learner meets is at work or in an interview. [Sourced — hiring-task research, rated a critical gap there] *Prevention:* one deliberate flaw in every blank-start task; repair rungs in the Excel, Python, and DE/ML ladders. 4. The given-metric shortcut. Exercises that always state the metric, the denominator, and the output shape, so the learner practices arithmetic while hiring tests definition. nodes.label: 4. Patterns to beat / avoid
nodes.text: 4. Patterns to beat / avoid Each item names the pattern, the platform(s) the audit found it on (pages accessed 2026-11-15), and the counter-design. These are the site's anti-requirements: a design review that finds any of them on Data From Zero has found a defect. 1. Auto-subscription traps (Coursera). Enrolling in one course silently subscribing the learner to a whole paid certificate — admitted in that platform's own FAQ, and the audit's clearest dark pattern. *Counter-design:* there is nothing to subscribe to, and the site says so. No accounts gate content; no trial exists to convert. 2. Hidden pricing (DataCamp, Dataquest, Codecademy). Homepages that say "free" loudly and a price nowhere; one platform's full price discoverable only in page metadata, its projects, quizzes, and certificate revealed as paid in a bottom-of-page upsell block. *Counter-design:* a free site weaponizes this contrast — "free, all of it, forever" stated where rivals state nothing, including on the pages for the parts incumbents paywall (projects, checkpoints, review sets). 3. nodes.label: 5. Visual teaching — the core lesson and the house sequence
nodes.text: 5. Visual teaching — the core lesson and the house sequence Confidence: High — the same pattern recurs across the visual explainers opened for the visual-teaching research (a visual introduction to probability and statistics; a visual introduction to machine learning in two parts; an interactive-article journal; two independent SQL join visualizers; a window-functions teaching guide; a Python step-through visualizer). All accessed 2026-11-15. The strongest visual teachers share one sequence, and it is the opposite of most incumbent courses: 1. Show the data moving first. The learner watches rows pair up, a distribution fill in, a split divide a scatterplot, or a variable change value — before any definition. 2. Name the mechanism in plain language while it is visible. The label lands on something the eye already tracked. 3. Only then show syntax or formula. Code and notation become a caption for a picture the learner already understands. 4. Let the learner change one thing and predict first. Drag a probability bar, edit a join key, move a split point, step one line forward — then compare the result to the prediction. House rule: no hard concept is introduced by syntax or formula alone. Every hard concept gets one canonical visual first. This exploits the dual-channel advantage the pedagogy research identifies — verbal and visual channels are separate and limited, so pairing a visual with concise text beats either alone — and it is the main antidote to math anxiety, because t…

nodes.text: 6. Technique catalog — mapped to the hard concepts Build-cost key: Static SVG = one hand-authored or generated vector diagram, no JavaScript required. CSS = layout, highlighting, or transition in styles alone. Interactive JS = a small client-side component; vanilla JavaScript or a tiny framework island, no server, no account. nodes.text: 8. Time-to-skill — the UX contribution Time-to-skill is one of the four tests the project is judged on, and the site's design — not only the curriculum's order — decides much of it. The mechanisms below are [Recommendation], each tied to an audit finding or a pedagogy finding; no speed multiplier is claimed anywhere (Section 4, item 6). - Zero setup, zero wall between arrival and first result. The audit's friction leaders are free and wall-less; every wall an incumbent adds (account before content, trial before syllabus, enterprise pitch before path cards) is time spent not learning. Data From Zero's first lesson starts on the page the beginner lands on, in the browser, with the dataset already there. - Decision time removed, not learning time. Path cards with decision metadata (Section 2, pattern 1), one linear order (no catalog search), and an always-visible "what next" convert the hours incumbents spend learners on *choosing* into hours spent *doing*. Choice overload is the largest incumbent's defining information-architecture problem in the audit; a single path is the fix. - Concepts arrive pre-understood. The visual-first sequence (Section 5) front-loads intuition so syntax is learned as a caption for a known picture, instead of being decoded and conceptualized simultaneously. nodes.label: 9.1 Budget rules
nodes.text: 9.1 Budget rules - Static first. Every visual ships as static SVG or CSS by default. JavaScript is added only where manipulation is the teaching mechanism (sliders, steppers, editable tables, small simulations). A page with no interactive concept ships no component JavaScript. - Island discipline. Each interactive visual is an isolated island that loads only on its own lesson page, hydrates lazily when it approaches the viewport, and never blocks the text — which must be fully readable before hydration. - No heavy animation libraries for simple work. CSS transitions and native scroll/intersection APIs cover steppers, highlights, and reveal effects. Reserve any animation library for a proven need on a flagship visual, loaded only on that page. Load animation code after the page is visible and initialize each section only when the reader scrolls near it. - Simulation caps. In-browser simulations (coin flips, sampling, tree growth) run on dozens to hundreds of points, precomputed where the sequence is fixed. Nothing animates thousands of DOM nodes; if a visual ever needs that scale, it belongs on a canvas element with a static SVG fallback, and that decision needs an explicit reason. - Fonts and images. Visuals are SVG and HTML, not raster screenshots, so they stay sharp, small, translatable, and theme-able. Do not ship a video file where a scrubbable SVG sequence teaches the same point. - Two spaces, one component library. Learn (spacious) and Reference (dense) render the same…

nodes.label: 9.2 Mobile rules
nodes.text: 9.2 Mobile rules - Design the visual for a narrow screen first. The audit flags roadmap.sh's dense node chart as inherently hard on a phone; Data From Zero's visuals must not repeat that. Tables in a visual keep at most a handful of columns; wide tables become stacked card pairs on small screens rather than shrinking to unreadable type. The roadmap map itself, on mobile, renders as the ordered stage list with the same metadata as the cards — the spatial chart is a desktop enhancement, never the only navigation. - Scrollytelling collapses vertically. The desktop pattern (text beside a pinned visual) becomes, on mobile, alternating text and visual blocks in one column, with the visual sticky only where it remains fully visible without covering the text. - Touch targets and controls. Steppers, sliders, and join-type switchers need large, thumb-reachable controls, and every drag interaction needs a tap/step alternative. Dragging a distribution bar or a regression line must also work as plus/minus steppers. - No hover-dependent teaching. Anything revealed on hover on desktop must be revealed on tap on mobile, and must never be the only place a definition or result appears. - Reduced motion and pausing. Respect the reader's reduced-motion preference: animations start paused or in their final state, autoplay is never the only mode, and every animation can be paused and stepped manually. This is an accessibility requirement, not a preference toggle. - Offline and low-bandwidth reali…

nodes.label: 9.3 Risks to avoid
nodes.text: 9.3 Risks to avoid - Animation as decoration. Movement that does not encode a change in the data teaches nothing and costs performance, battery, and attention. House test: if removing the motion loses no information, remove the motion. - Simulation sprawl. Each interactive is code that must be maintained, translated, and tested in two languages and two site spaces. Ten excellent, reused components beat forty one-off interactives. Build a small component library — table-pairing, table-stepper, distribution, scatterplot-and-line, state-tracer, bucket-grouping — and compose lessons from it. - Canvas-only or JS-only content. Content locked inside a canvas or available only after hydration is invisible to search, print, translation review, and screen readers. Every visual needs a text equivalent that states its conclusion in words. - Screenshot teaching assets. A screenshot of a real spreadsheet, editor, or product UI cannot be stepped, highlighted, localized, or re-themed, and it ages with the vendor's UI. Teaching visuals are drawn components (HTML/CSS/SVG), per Section 6.3's canonical-visual rule. ---

nodes.label: 1.3 What the demand evidence does and does not justify
nodes.text: 1.3 What the demand evidence does and does not justify The Excel → SQL → Python order stands, but on two legs, not one: 1. Market leg (corrected): Excel and SQL are effectively tied at the top of analyst demand, with order varying by sample; Python follows for analysts and leads for scientists. Starting with either Excel or SQL is market-defensible. 2. Learning-sequence leg: Excel is the fastest first win for the path's core audience — workers who already live in spreadsheets — because it builds on an existing mental model (tables, formulas, summaries) before introducing a query language and then a programming language. That pedagogical argument holds regardless of which of Excel or SQL tops a given sample. Do not cite a false unanimity to defend the order. The corrected #1-or-#2 formulation is strong enough. Salary context for the home market, from a Vietnamese career guide opened in the research: entry-level data analyst roles in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi are listed at 10–16 million VND per month for fresher and junior positions. Against that income, annual subscriptions priced in the hundreds of US dollars are a structural barrier, not a minor inconvenience — a point that returns in Section 5. ---

nodes.label: 2. The Interview Layer: How Hiring Actually Tests
nodes.text: 2. The Interview Layer: How Hiring Actually Tests Hiring does not test topics in syllabus order. It tests judgment under ambiguity, on messy data, against a clock, out loud. Platforms mostly test recognition and reproduction on clean data, untimed and silently. Almost every gap below traces back to that difference. A curriculum that teaches the same beginner topics inside hiring-shaped tasks closes most of the gap without adding new topics.

nodes.label: 2.1 SQL interviews: ten patterns and a five-rung ladder
nodes.text: 2.1 SQL interviews: ten patterns and a five-rung ladder Four independent interview sources converge on the same structure. A typical data SQL interview hands the candidate a small schema and a business-flavored prompt, watches the query being written live or in a timed assessment, and scores reasoning as much as result: clarifying the definition, stating the output grain, handling ties, duplicates, and null values out loud, and writing readable structure with common table expressions instead of one nested block. PostgreSQL is the safe default dialect in the guidance opened, because interviews usually grade logic over dialect trivia and allow lookup leeway on date and time syntax. The ten pattern families (ordered by when they tend to appear in a loop): 1. Filtered retrieval — return or count rows meeting layered conditions, including conditions in another table, in text, or in time. 2. Aggregation and conditional aggregation — summarize by group; compute several metrics in one pass; turn conditions into metrics with conditional logic inside aggregates. 3. Joins, including negative and self-referential cases — combine tables without inflating counts; find rows with no match; compare rows within the same table (for example employees against managers). 4. Top-N and ranking per group — pick the best, nth, or top few rows inside each group, with an explicit tie policy. The choice among row-number, rank, and dense-rank behavior is the test. 5. Time comparison — rolling averages, l…

nodes.label: 2.2 Excel hiring tests: three formats, ten task types
nodes.text: 2.2 Excel hiring tests: three formats, ten task types There is no single standard Excel test. Employers use three formats: 1. Short multiple-choice screens — what a formula returns, which reference type survives copying, which feature solves a stated problem. Timed in minutes; tests recognition and speed. 2. Hands-on simulations — perform the task inside a spreadsheet-like environment; the system checks the resulting state. 3. Live or take-home workbook tasks — work through a real file, watched live or submitted, where the deliverable is a workbook another person can audit, reuse, and trust. A learner trained only to pick the right menu item is prepared for the first format and exposed in the other two. The ten task types: 1. Tidy and total a list — sort, filter, and total over the correct range, with live formulas rather than hand rearrangement. 2. Fix a broken sheet — find entry errors such as a date stored as text, correct them without breaking formatting, make the sheet print correctly. 3. Look values up across sheets — bring a price or attribute in by code, including codes that do not match, and handle the not-found case deliberately instead of leaving raw errors. 4. Summarize with a PivotTable and answer in words — build the pivot and state the finding. Classic trap: the pivot shows a count instead of a sum because the amount column is stored as text. 5. Clean a messy export — split combined fields, trim stray spaces, remove duplicates on the right key columns, keep th…

nodes.label: 2.3 Analytics case questions: six families
nodes.text: 2.3 Analytics case questions: six families The case round tests metric judgment, not calculation. Calculating the wrong thing correctly is scored as a failure. Prompts are intentionally ambiguous — terms such as active user, retention, and engagement are left undefined on purpose — and the expected first move is clarification, not code. 1. Define the metric — measure the success of a feature, product, or checkout page. Scored on starting from user and business goals, naming one primary metric plus guardrail metrics that must not degrade, and matching the metric to the goal. 2. Diagnose a movement — a metric dropped last week; what do you do? Scored on a fixed order: verify the signal is real (tracking change, outage, holiday, definition change), segment (platform, region, channel, device, new versus returning), locate the funnel step or driver, form a testable hypothesis, recommend a next step. 3. Design an experiment — test a new flow or feature. Scored on hypothesis, randomization unit, primary and guardrail metrics, sample-size and duration reasoning including covering a full weekly cycle, success criteria stated in advance, and pitfalls such as stopping early on a first significant result. 4. Judge a trade-off or read a result — engagement rose but revenue fell; ship it? Or: the experiment shows a lift; do you believe it? Scored on weighing short against long term, checking data and randomization before celebrating, and proposing an explicit decision rule. 5. Interpret g…

nodes.label: 2.4 The Python round and the take-home
nodes.text: 2.4 The Python round and the take-home For analyst and scientist roles, the Python round is largely the SQL patterns translated into pandas, performed live on a small dataset and judged on idiomatic vectorized code as well as correct output: selection and boolean masking; merge as the join, with relationship validation, origin indicators, and predicting the output row count before running — including row multiplication from duplicate keys on both sides; groupby as a system, including transform for group-level values broadcast back to rows (filling a missing value with its own group's mean rather than the global mean, which gives materially different results) and grouped ranking and lag (an ungrouped shift leaks the previous customer's last value into the next customer's first row); reshaping, where pivot refuses duplicate pairs and pivot-table aggregates them; share-of-total and top-N per group with an explicit tie policy; and cleaning, type awareness, and vectorization over row-wise loops. Engineering tracks add pipeline-shaped work: ingesting messy files and nested payloads, validating keys, snapshot diffing, and writing output a rerun cannot break. Take-homes cut across all four formats above and are a genre with learnable conventions: - Shape: a dataset plus business questions, completed asynchronously. nodes.text: 2.5 The gap table, compressed Fifteen gaps were cataloged in the underlying research. The three critical ones are not advanced topics; they are beginner topics taught with the judgment layer stripped out: - Metric definition (critical): platforms give the metric in the exercise statement; hiring requires choosing, defining, and defending it before computing. - Ambiguity (critical): platform prompts are fully specified with one intended answer; hiring prompts are deliberately vague, and clarifying questions and stated assumptions are scored behavior. - Data cleanliness (critical): platforms supply clean, typed, deduplicated tables; hiring supplies duplicates, nulls, text-stored numbers, late events, and many-to-many joins that inflate totals — and spotting and handling them is the test. nodes.label: 3.1 The cross-track rule
nodes.text: 3.1 The cross-track rule Every track source states the same rule in some form: proof of work outweighs credentials, depth outweighs count, and a live or runnable artifact outweighs a description. A hiring manager may spend only about 30 seconds on an initial portfolio review, looking for immediate evidence the candidate can solve a real problem, explain their thinking, and show results that matter to stakeholders. The three screening pillars are technical competence, business acumen, and communication. The consensus count is 3–5 polished, well-documented projects, recurring independently across analyst, science, and platform sources. The one deliberate exception is Data Engineering, where the bar is 2–3 deep projects. For ML/AI Engineering, one portfolio guide reports a pattern of 4–6 deployed projects spanning retrieval, an agentic workflow, an MLOps or deployment project, and one fine-tune as consistently landing interviews. Counts are targets for depth, not quotas to fill with clones. GitHub hygiene is part of the evidence for every technical track: a small number of pinned, well-organized repositories with clear READMEs, meaningful commit history, and no clutter of tutorial repositories burying the real work. For engineering roles the profile is treated as due diligence — the resume is the pitch, the repository is the verification.

nodes.label: 3.2 What platforms assign, and why it is not enough
nodes.text: 3.2 What platforms assign, and why it is not enough Platform work falls into four patterns: - Short guided browser projects (DataCamp pattern): scoped tasks on pre-loaded data, from about 30 minutes to about 1 hour for guided SQL projects, with the task, dataset, and success check all supplied. Structural limit: the learner practices execution inside a known frame rather than framing a problem, and datasets that cannot be downloaded leave finished work trapped inside the platform. The platform's own portfolio guidance names the fix — add a business question, a table description or diagram, each query with output and a one-line finding, a limitations paragraph, and one change made beyond the brief — and advises that three projects with clear write-ups outweigh twelve that stop at the last query. - Longer guided projects on downloadable, messy data (Dataquest pattern): realistic scenarios on real, messy, downloadable datasets, commonly 4–8 hours for beginner projects, rebuildable locally and publishable with documentation. This pattern transfers; the 3–5 polished-project standard is stated here as well. - Certificate capstones (Coursera/IBM pattern): one integrative end project. The older science shape runs a full methodology loop once, on a supplied problem. The newer engineering shape additionally demands governance, operations planning, and an architecture narrative — much closer to what engineering hiring screens for. - Competition work (Kaggle pattern): nothing is assigne…

nodes.label: 3.3 Per-track hiring bars
nodes.text: 3.3 Per-track hiring bars Data Analyst. Screened for visible fluency — SQL first as the near-universal requirement, plus Excel or Sheets, one BI tool (Tableau or Power BI are the recurring pair), and increasingly Python — and for at least one full-cycle project: question, data, cleaning and querying, visualization, insight, recommendation. Minimum shape: at least one SQL project, one Python project, and one dashboard project, plus a published dashboard a non-technical reader can use and a README stating what was done, what data was used, and what was found. Visible messy-data work carries disproportionate weight, because cleaning is a large share of real analyst work and the skill most underrepresented in beginner portfolios. Weak framing loses: a title that reads like a manager's question beats a title that names a dataset. Data Engineer. Screened for 2–3 deep projects that mimic a real pipeline end to end — a real problem statement, realistic messy or multi-source data, and a multi-stage design from ingestion through transformation and storage to serving — over many shallow demos. Reviewers scan a recognizable stack (orchestration, distributed processing, transformation and modeling, a cloud warehouse, Git) for how tools were applied, not merely that they appear. Engineering quality is scored directly: modular code, a reproducibility file or container definition, error handling and logging, and thought about reruns, mid-pipeline failure, and duplicate prevention. nodes.text: 3.4 The ten gaps between assigned and expected 1. Problem framing — supplied versus self-chosen and scoped, with stakeholder and decision named. 2. Data realism — clean, single-source, sometimes non-downloadable versus messy, multi-source, self-collected, with documented cleaning. 3. Originality — the same project completed by every learner in a cohort versus work that does not look identical to hundreds of other applicants. 4. Deployment and operations — ends at a notebook or in-platform dashboard versus a live artifact with container, CI/CD, monitoring, or an incident plan. Critical for ML/AI; high for Data Engineering. 5. Engineering workflow — solo browser work versus Git history, branches and pull requests, tests, CI, and a reproducible environment. Critical for Analytics Engineering, Data Engineering, and ML/AI. 6. nodes.label: 3.5 The capstone ladder for Data From Zero
nodes.text: 3.5 The capstone ladder for Data From Zero Design rules for all tracks: - Four rungs per track. Rung 1: guided core (supplied question and data). Rung 2: messy-data rebuild (same skill, self-sourced or deliberately dirty data). Rung 3: end-to-end build (full track workflow, with tests, evaluation, and documentation as appropriate). Rung 4: capstone (self-framed problem, deployed or published artifact, case-study write-up). Learners publish Rungs 2–4; Rung 1 is practice. - One portfolio packet at every published rung: public repository; README opening with a one-sentence business problem; architecture or workflow diagram where relevant; how-to-run instructions; results in business terms; a limitations paragraph; and a beyond-the-brief note stating what the learner chose or changed. - One domain thread per learner, picked early and carried through at least Rungs 3–4, so the finished portfolio reads as a coherent story for one industry's hiring managers. - Review like a hiring manager: a two-minute scan test first (can a reviewer state the problem, approach, and result from the README alone?), then a deep review against the track bar in Section 3.3. Data Analyst ladder. Rung 1: guided SQL and exploration — a supplied business question set on one dataset, then a Python exploration of a second. Rung 2: messy-data cleaning story — combine two inconsistent sources, document every cleaning decision, analyze the combined result. Rung 3: dashboard plus recommendation — an interactive…

nodes.label: 4. Certification Map: What the Big Exams Test, and How the Path Aligns
nodes.text: 4. Certification Map: What the Big Exams Test, and How the Path Aligns Certifications are used here as public blueprints — checklists of what established issuers consider testable — never as lesson sources, and alignment never promises exam readiness from any single module. Eight certifications were mapped in full in the underlying research. Prices, durations, and scores are stated only where an official page or exam guide opened in the research stated them; where verification could not confirm a figure from an official page, the figure is labeled or omitted, by design.

nodes.label: 4.1 The eight certifications in brief
nodes.text: 4.1 The eight certifications in brief 1. Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate (Google, via Coursera) — entry level. A multi-course program, not a single proctored exam. The Coursera program page describes nine courses and over 180 hours of instruction, completable in under six months at under 10 hours per week, at $49 per month in the United States and Canada after a free trial. (Other Google and review pages state different course counts and hour totals for this program; the figures here are the Coursera program page's own.) It tests the full analyst workflow — framing a question, preparing and cleaning data in spreadsheets and SQL, analyzing, and sharing findings with visualizations, dashboards, and presentations, primarily with Tableau — plus introductory Python for analysis. The current program teaches Python and explicitly does not cover R. Its capstone-style case study is the only end-to-end portfolio artifact required by any certification in this map. It does not emphasize deep statistics, machine learning, pipelines, or cloud platforms. 2. Microsoft Office Specialist: Excel Associate, Exam MO-210 (Microsoft, via Certiport) — associate level. A performance-based exam taken live inside Excel. Five domains, with weightings confirmed from Microsoft's official skills outline: manage worksheets and workbooks (25–30%); manage data cells and ranges (25–30%); manage tables and table data (10–15%); perform operations using formulas and functions (15–20%), including r…

nodes.label: 4.2 What the cross-certification matrix shows
nodes.text: 4.2 What the cross-certification matrix shows - No single certification covers the whole beginner-to-job path. Analyst credentials barely touch cloud engineering; engineering credentials barely touch storytelling, and the AWS engineering guide excludes drawing business conclusions outright. Following only one blueprint leaves a visible hole. - Cleaning, SQL, and modeling recur everywhere hands-on work is tested. Every hands-on certification in the map rewards profiling and fixing data, querying with SQL, and structuring data into tables with clear relationships. Those are safe universal bets for core curriculum time. - Security and governance grow with level; they do not start at zero. Beginner material frames ethics, privacy, and appropriate sharing; associate material adds access control and row-level security; professional material adds encryption keys, sovereignty, and federated governance. The topic should spiral, not appear once.

nodes.label: 4.3 Alignment recommendations
nodes.text: 4.3 Alignment recommendations 1. Anchor the Excel block to the MO-210 blueprint, then go one step past it. Use the five domains as the completeness checklist, weight practice the way the exam does (more time on workbooks, formatting, and ranges than on exotic formulas), and add PivotTables and lookups immediately after, flagged honestly as post-Associate, Expert-direction skills. A timed, live-in-Excel practical of about 50 minutes mirrors the credential's format without using any of its tasks — with the duration understood as per secondary guides, as noted above. 2. Make the single SQL block satisfy three blueprints at once. The same block can serve the Google certificate's query-to-clean-and-analyze workflow, DP-900's relational concepts (features, normalization, common statements and objects), and the Google Associate Data Practitioner's expectation of writing SQL in a warehouse to answer a business question. Add one relational-versus-non-relational decision lesson, and end the block with a warehouse-style exercise on a larger read-only dataset with a short written conclusion. 3. Position Python as the Google certificate now does — after spreadsheets and SQL. Python for analysis in notebooks, as a productivity upgrade on problems learners have already solved in Excel and SQL, with no cloud SDKs, pipeline frameworks, or model training in the first block. End the core path with one end-to-end case — question, preparation, cleaning, analysis, visualization, recommendation —…

nodes.text: 5. Positioning and Viral Lessons

nodes.label: 5.1 What incumbents promise, and who is left out
nodes.text: 5.1 What incumbents promise, and who is left out - DataCamp promises interactive in-browser coding from lesson one, a path for every goal, career tracks, and exam certifications. Its free tier is the first chapter of every course only. Use one dated price formulation everywhere: list price about $28 per month billed annually; the pricing page simultaneously promotes an $11 per month special price (read 2026-11-15). DataCamp's own pages state different catalog and track hour totals in different places, so no single total is presented in this package as the total. Instruction is in English; subtitles do not teach a learner to read an English error message or write an English query comment. - Coursera promises university and brand-name credentials and career outcomes. Its free mode is a preview without the credential, and its format is video-lecture-first — learners who need doing more than watching, and learners for whom the certificate is not the point, are underserved. - Dataquest promises learning without videos, code from lesson one, real datasets, and honest time estimates. Content is in English only, and it offers enrollment in a path rather than a map of everything. - freeCodeCamp is 100% free as a public charity, with courses, projects, and certifications. Its core curriculum is developer-first, its data science offering is one branch among many measured in years, and it offers no spreadsheet on-ramp for Office workers. - Codecademy promises interactive lessons, guided…

nodes.label: 5.2 What actually gets shared: seven mechanics
nodes.text: 5.2 What actually gets shared: seven mechanics 1. A picture of the whole journey. A static roadmap image is screenshot-able, printable, and forwardable in a way a course catalog never is. The developer-roadmap repository behind roadmap.sh showed about 372,000 stars on its page when opened for this research, and its README ships share badges for major social platforms — the project asks to be shared. The artifact that spreads is the map, not the lesson. 2. Free, ordered, and open — creators amplify it for you. A free ordered path is content other creators can make videos about. The OSSU data-science curriculum repository stands at about 22K stars (November 2026), and creator videos walking viewers through free curriculum repositories reliably field one dominant comment request: the link. (For scale, the companion OSSU computer-science repository stands at about 211K stars, November 2026 — counts are date-stamped approximations because live counters drift weekly.) Distribution of this kind cannot be bought; it is earned by being safely recommendable. 3. No account, no paywall, no upsell at the moment of need. Free practice resources earn their place in recommendation lists with the same reasoning: short explanation, exercise against a real database, instant feedback — and no signup ambush that would embarrass the person who recommended them. 4. A public commitment device with a named handle. The long-running 100-days-of-coding pattern has two rules — practice at least an hour…

nodes.label: 5.3 Five positioning moves incumbents cannot copy quickly
nodes.text: 5.3 Five positioning moves incumbents cannot copy quickly 1. Vietnamese-first, not subtitled. Build the path natively in Vietnamese — explanations and analogies in Vietnamese, job vocabulary kept in English — with the English edition as the parallel track. Incumbents cannot copy this quickly because their content factories are English-first pipelines whose non-English offer tops out at subtitles over English exercises, or English only outright. Retooling thousands of interactive exercises into native instruction is a rebuild, not a toggle, and a single home market that is too small to justify that rebuild at subscription price points is exactly the right size to be a focused site's home market. 2. The whole path free, with no account and no funnel, as a stated public good. Not a free tier: the entire Excel → SQL → Python → tracks path, drills and projects included, readable and usable without signup, under CC BY 4.0. Incumbents cannot copy this because their revenue is the paywall — a first-chapter free tier and a preview-without-credential free mode are deliberate sampling funnels, and matching everything-free would cannibalize the subscription base that funds them. The one large exception needed a charity model and a decade, and still offers no data-first, Excel-first path. 3. One committed order with deadlines and pass/fail checkpoints — an anti-catalog. Exactly one path, in one order, with week-sized stages and a you-may-proceed-when-you-can-do-this gate at each stage. M…

nodes.label: 5.4 Honest limits
nodes.text: 5.4 Honest limits Incumbent learner counts are the organizations' own homepage claims and are reported as claims, not audited figures. List prices rotate with promotions, which is why Section 5.1 fixes one dated formulation instead of quoting whichever price a given page happens to show. No search-trend data is claimed anywhere in this file: trend tooling could not be opened during the research, and job-market evidence was used instead — arguably the better signal for a careers-first site, but a trends pass remains an open follow-up. And the demand table in Section 1 should be rebuilt, not merely re-dated, at each curriculum cycle: its own rows show that shares move materially between samples only a year or two apart. ---

nodes.label: How the branches build on the core
nodes.text: How the branches build on the core - Data Analyst applies the core: SQL L4 patterns and pandas to scoped reporting, retention reading, a dashboard design and model lesson, a BI tool lesson, A/B readout, case practice, a take-home and a case study. - Data Engineer takes `python-notebook-to-script`, `sql-modify-data-transactions`, and the core cloud, warehouse and Git lessons to idempotent loads, quality checks, Airflow, backfills, Spark and a design-and-defend capstone. - Data Scientist takes the evaluation trio (framing, leakage, metrics) plus regression and tests, then algorithms, cross-validation, feature engineering, interpretation, forecasting and experiment analysis. - Analytics Engineer takes SQL CTEs and windows, Git review, and the two data-modeling lessons. Slowly changing dimensions and views are deferred here from the core and SQL on purpose. - ML Engineer takes the core evaluation trio and the AI literacy lesson. It also takes three DS lessons (see the cross-branch edges below). - Cross-branch rule. Branches may not depend on each other, with one whitelisted exception: ML Engineer lists three Data Scientist lessons (feature engineering, cross-validation, gradient boosting) as prerequisites, because a concept has one home URL. `validate.mjs` fails any other cross-branch edge.

nodes.label: How the map is built
nodes.text: How the map is built - One idea per lesson, one visual per lesson. Each lesson names its canonical static visual (`visual:`). Playbook steppers and sliders (03 §7) are written as static frame sequences, because lessons ship no JavaScript. - Order follows prerequisites (D25). The graph module reports no cycles and no order violations. No lesson depends on a later stage. Only the first Excel lesson has no prerequisite; the first lesson of each later stage depends on the stage before it. - Stage sizes. Excel 22, SQL 30, Python 25, core 25, branches 11 to 12. Seven lessons are marked `[stretch]`: nothing on the main path depends on them, so they can be cut or deferred. Without them: 154 lessons.

nodes.label: Ordering logic per stage
nodes.text: Ordering logic per stage Excel (22). Grid and tidy layout, formulas, references, then types and locale before any aggregation (a PivotTable on text-stored numbers is the classic failure, so "numbers are not numbers until you check" comes before pivots). Then tables, logic, conditional totals, lookups, text and dates, error triage, and a cleaning workflow. PivotTables, charts and a one-screen report close the block. Two bridges point forward: `excel-sheets-query-bridge` (QUERY as a preview of SQL) and `excel-xlookup` (the spreadsheet rehearsal for joins). The AI lesson comes last because it is gated on formulas learned unaided. SQL (30), one complete block. Tables, keys and grain, then retrieval, filtering, NULL, types, CASE. Aggregation and GROUP BY come before joins, so every join lesson can verify its row count with COUNT. Joins run inner, left and anti, then fan-out as a critique lesson, then self and multi-table joins. Then subqueries, CTEs (the house style from there on) and set logic. Window functions come last in the query half, with the hiring patterns after them: top-N, LAG and LEAD, deduplication, funnels, cohorts, date spine. Design basics (constraints, writes and transactions, normalization, indexes) finish the block before Python starts. The AI lesson is last. Pattern families 1 to 10 of 05 §2.1 are all covered. Python (25). One bridge lesson answers the same cafe question in Sheets, SQL and Python. Ten language lessons follow, taught for reading and recognition…

nodes.label: Why some stages exceed 12 to 20 lessons
nodes.text: Why some stages exceed 12 to 20 lessons - SQL (30, 28 without stretch). 00 §1 makes SQL one block: no later "advanced SQL". The inventory has 260+ items and ten hiring pattern families. Merging lessons breaks one idea per lesson. Twenty-eight lessons at about 25 minutes is about 12 hours. - Python (25). Three jobs in one stage: language (10), pandas (11), workflow and automation (4). Only `python-environments-and-pip` is stretch; the APIs and AI lessons are prerequisites of later lessons. - Core (25). Six areas mandated by the brief, each needed by all five branches. Statistics alone is 11. - Excel (22, 20 without stretch). The Excel hiring task types (05 §2.2) need ten distinct skills, and Vietnamese locale traps add two.

nodes.label: Principles (in priority order)
nodes.text: Principles (in priority order) 1. Permanence. Every published URL keeps working forever. Content outlives the framework. 2. Stability & speed. Static site, minimal JavaScript, works with JS disabled, fast on a phone. 3. Academic quality. Versioned, citable (DOI), sourced, dated, reviewed. 4. Beginner-first. Audience knows only Microsoft Office; most read on phones. 5. Delight, sparingly. GSAP motion only on the homepage (D28). ---

nodes.label: Content production (replaces migration, D24)
nodes.text: Content production (replaces migration, D24) Content is written from scratch; `johnha912/data-odyssey` is not migrated. 1. Curriculum map. Research proposes every lesson per stage (id, slug, title, order, level, duration, objectives, prerequisites, key sources). The owner approves the map once; slugs then become permanent (§3). 2. Stubs. Approved lessons are created as `status: draft` files (never deployed, D18). The build validates ids, prerequisites and cycles from day one. 3. Writing. The owner writes the lesson text. The team adds or completes frontmatter, exercises and solutions, notebooks, Google Sheets templates, datasets (§7), `Term` links and sources, and keeps the build green. 4. Publishing. The owner reviews and sets `status: published`. Vietnamese translations follow in later PRs (§8). 5. Release. Tag `v1.0.0` once the four core stages are published; enable Zenodo; publish `CITATION.cff` (§9).

nodes.label: Slug rules
nodes.text: Slug rules - Lowercase English, kebab-case, ASCII only: `/sql/window-functions/`. Vietnamese pages reuse the English slug. - No numbers, dates or versions in slugs. Order comes from `order` in frontmatter. - Always a trailing slash (`trailingSlash: 'always'`). - The slug is derived from the file name; the file name is the slug.

nodes.label: Change rules
nodes.text: Change rules - Never rename or delete a published URL. If a rename is unavoidable: 1. add an entry to `src/redirects.ts` (old → new), 2. keep the lesson `id` unchanged (§5.1), 3. note it in `CHANGELOG.md`. - A retired page stays online with `status: deprecated` and a link to its replacement. - Anchors (`#heading-id`) on reference pages are part of the contract — headings there are not renamed casually.

nodes.label: Linking inside content
nodes.text: Linking inside content - Internal links are root-relative (`/sql/joins/`), never absolute (`https://datafromzero.github.io/…`). - Link to other lessons by path; the build validates every internal link (§12). ---

nodes.label: Information architecture
nodes.text: Information architecture ``` datafromzero ├─ Learn (Study mode — open, quiet, one idea per screen) │ ├─ 1 Excel / Sheets → 2 SQL → 3 Python → 4 Advanced core │ └─ Branches: Data Analyst · Data Engineer · Data Scientist · ML/AI Engineer ├─ Reference (Book mode — indexed, compact, searchable) │ ├─ Glossary │ ├─ Syntax: Excel functions · SQL keywords · pandas │ ├─ Statistics formulas │ └─ Careers (4 guides) ├─ Stories (history, explainers, visualizations — motion allowed) ├─ Datasets └─ About · Cite · Changelog · License · Privacy ``` Sidebar order and grouping are generated from frontmatter (`stage`, `order`), never hand-maintained. ---

nodes.label: Content model
nodes.text: Content model Schemas are registered in `src/content.config.ts` and defined in `src/lib/content-schemas.ts`; validation runs on every build (`src/lib/content-validation.ts`). Adding an optional field = MINOR change. Adding a required field, renaming or removing a field = MAJOR change + migration script. Rules for every type (D17): - `id` is lowercase kebab-case (`a-z`, `0-9`, `-`) and unique across all content types (an English page and its Vietnamese translation share one id). - The file's folder decides its type (paths in the headings below). A file nested deeper than its type allows fails the build. - Every id reference must point to an existing entry of the right type. - `sources[].url` and `sheet` must be `http(s)` URLs. - The build reports all problems at once, naming the file and field, and fails.

nodes.label: Lesson (`src/content/docs/{stage}/{slug}.md`)
nodes.text: Lesson (`src/content/docs/{stage}/{slug}.md`) ```yaml --- id: sql-joins # permanent internal key; never changes, even if the slug does title: Joining tables description: Combine rows from two tables with INNER and LEFT JOIN. # ≤ 160 chars, used for SEO/social stage: sql # excel | sql | python | core | data-analyst | data-engineer | # data-scientist | ml-engineer order: 40 # sort key inside the stage; use gaps of 10 so lessons can be inserted level: beginner # beginner | intermediate | advanced duration: 25 # minutes, integer objectives: # 2–5 items, each starts with a verb - Explain what a join key is - Write an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN prerequisites: # lesson ids (not URLs); validated at build time - sql-select-basics datasets: [cafe-sales] # dataset names (§7); optional notebook: notebooks/sql/sql-joins.ipynb # optional; drives the "Open in Colab" button sheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/…/copy # optional; Excel stage "Make a copy" link reviewed: 2026-11-15 # last date the content was checked for correctness sources: # at least 1; documentation, papers, books - title: PostgreSQL documentation — Joined tables url: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html status: published # draft | published | deprecated replaced_by: null # lesson id, required when status = deprecated --- ``` - `stage` must match the lesson's folder. - `status: draft` lessons are built only in local dev, never deployed (D18). A published or deprecated lesson may not list a draft in `prerequisites` or `replaced_by`. - A deprecated lesson shows a notice linking to `replaced_by` (§3.3). Rendered at the top of every lesson: level · duration · last reviewed, then Objectives and Before this lesson (prerequisite links). Rendered at the bottom: Unlocks next (the lessons that list this one in `prerequisites`, drafts excluded, in the reader's language, computed at build time without JavaScript; hidden when empty), Sources, Cite this lesson, Suggest an edit, Report an issue, prev/next. - Inside one stage, `order` must be a topological order of `prerequisites`: a prerequisite in the same stage has a smaller `order`. Prerequisite cycles fail the check (`scripts/check-graph.ts`, §12).

nodes.label: Reference entry (`src/content/docs/reference/{area}/{slug}.md`)
nodes.text: Reference entry (`src/content/docs/reference/{area}/{slug}.md`) ```yaml --- id: ref-sql-group-by title: GROUP BY area: sql # excel | sql | pandas | stats summary: Groups rows that share values so aggregates are computed per group. syntax: | # optional, shown in a code block at the top SELECT col, AGG(x) FROM t GROUP BY col; see_also: [ref-sql-having, glossary-aggregate] # ids used_in: [sql-aggregation] # lesson ids; optional (can also be computed) reviewed: 2026-11-15 sources: [ … ] --- ``` Reference pages use a fixed section order: Syntax → Parameters → Examples → Common mistakes → See also. `area` must match the folder. `see_also` is required (an empty list is allowed); its ids may be reference entries or glossary terms. `used_in` must name existing lessons that are not drafts (D18).

nodes.label: Authoring components
nodes.text: Authoring components The only components content may use. Each must degrade to readable static HTML without JS. | Component | Purpose | No-JS fallback | |---|---|---| | `<Exercise id="sql-joins-1">` … `</Exercise>` | Numbered exercise block | Plain block | | `<Solution>` … `</Solution>` (inside `Exercise`) | Hidden answer, "Show solution" | Native `<details>` | | `<OpenInColab />` | Button from the lesson's `notebook` field | Plain link | | `<OpenInSheets />` | "Make a copy" button from the lesson's `sheet` field | Plain link | | `<Term id="glossary-primary-key">primary key</Term>` | Inline glossary link with short definition | Plain link | | Starlight `<Aside>` (note / tip / caution / danger) | Callouts | Built in | | `$…$`, `$$…$$` | Math (KaTeX) | MathML | Rules: - No other components or raw `<script>` in content. New components are added here first (MINOR change). - Components are available in every `.mdx` file without import lines (D21). The build fails, naming the file and line, on any `import`/`export` in content, any component not in this table, any `<script>`, event-handler attribute (`on…=`), `set:html` or `javascript:` URL (in `.md` or `.mdx`), a `Solution` outside an `Exercise`, or math inside a heading. - `Term` shows the definition as a native popover, with no JS: opened by hover/focus where interest invokers exist (`interestfor`), otherwise by a small "?" button next to the link (`popovertarget`, tap or click). Both dismiss with Esc or an outside click; the link always goes to the glossary page. - A literal dollar sign in prose must be written `\$`; otherwise `$…$` is read as math. - Exercise ids are permanent (`{lesson-id}-{n}`) so teachers can reference "Exercise sql-joins-2".

nodes.label: Datasets
nodes.text: Datasets ``` datasets/ cafe-sales/ v1/ orders.csv customers.csv README.md # description, columns, types, row counts, how it was generated, license schema.yaml # machine-readable column definitions ``` - A small set of synthetic datasets the author creates, reused from Excel through Python so learners see the same data in every tool. No personal data. - Immutable once released. A change in columns or values = new folder `v2/`; `v1/` stays forever, so old notebooks and spreadsheets keep working. - Notebooks load data from a release-tag URL, not `main`: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datafromzero/datafromzero.github.io/v1.0.0/datasets/cafe-sales/v1/orders.csv` - Each dataset also ships an `.xlsx` (Excel stage) and a `.sql` load script (SQL stage) generated by a script in `scripts/`. - License: CC BY 4.0. Notebooks: `notebooks/{stage}/{lesson-id}.ipynb`, opened via `https://colab.research.google.com/github/datafromzero/datafromzero.github.io/blob/main/notebooks/…`. Notebooks are cleared of outputs before commit (CI check). ---

nodes.text: Internationalization > Paused (D30). The site is English only until the owner reactivates this section. Nothing below is > built meanwhile: no `vi` locale, and any page under `src/content/docs/vi/` fails the build. The rules stay > as written for when Vietnamese returns (set `VI_ENABLED` in `src/site.ts`, remove the `/vi/` redirects). - Starlight i18n with `root` locale English and `vi` locale. UI strings translated in `src/content/i18n/vi.json`. - Vietnamese files mirror English paths: `src/content/docs/vi/sql/joins.md` with the same `id`. - Untranslated pages fall back to English with Starlight's "not yet translated" notice. - A translation records `translated_from_version` (curriculum version it was translated from) so stale translations can be listed. It is required on every Vietnamese page of a typed collection (§5), and the page must have an English counterpart at the mirrored path with the same `id`. - Code, SQL keywords and dataset column names stay in English in both languages. ---

nodes.label: Versioning, citation, changelog
nodes.text: Versioning, citation, changelog - Curriculum version (SemVer), tagged on GitHub as `vX.Y.Z`: - MAJOR — curriculum restructure, a required schema change, or any URL redirect batch - MINOR — new lessons, reference entries, datasets, components, optional fields - PATCH — corrections, clarifications, link fixes - Each GitHub Release is archived by Zenodo (GitHub integration) → one concept DOI (always latest) + one DOI per version. - `CITATION.cff` at repo root (title, author, version, date, concept DOI, license). Updated on every release. - `/cite/` page: APA + BibTeX for the whole work, generated at build time from `CITATION.cff` (the build fails if its `version` differs from `package.json`); the DOI line reads "after the first release" until Zenodo exists, then shows the concept DOI and per-version DOIs. - Every lesson footer shows Cite this lesson: author, year (from `reviewed`), title, site, curriculum version, URL. Static pages cannot know when they were read, so a note asks the reader to add their access date (D20). - `CHANGELOG.md` follows *Keep a Changelog*; `/changelog/` renders it (single source, no copy); `/license/` shows `LICENSE` and `LICENSE-CONTENT` the same way. - The site footer shows the current version and its DOI badge. ---

Per frame: one canvas redraw, no DOM reads or writes (the size comes from a ResizeObserver, the color is read once per theme), within the SPEC §12 frame budget. Opening a card fades the figure in (transform and opacity only). The tween never reads styles after the click's DOM changes: GSAP keeps the canvas's transform in its cache (no clearProps), so the click costs no forced layout. The panel's lines lift in with CSS (home.css, .cr-detail.is-picked). await afterNextFrame(); // a frame slot of its own for the setup a long gap (tab in the background, a stall) must not make the figure jump: at most a quarter second
